question: What term describes a microorganism that causes disease?

options.A: Commensal
options.B: Eukaryote
options.C: Pathogen
options.D: Saprophyte

explanation: A pathogen is specifically defined as any disease-causing agent or microorganism. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h1)

question: When does an opportunistic pathogen cause an infection?

options.A: When the organism enters through the skin
options.B: When the patient eats contaminated food
options.C: When the host immune system is weakened
options.D: When antibiotics are taken in high doses

explanation: Opportunistic organisms take advantage of lowered host defenses to cause illness. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h1)

question: What color do Gram-positive bacteria appear after staining?

options.A: Green
options.B: Pink
options.C: Red
options.D: Purple

explanation: Gram-positive bacteria retain the crystal violet dye and appear purple under light microscopy. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h2)

question: Why do viruses differ fundamentally from bacteria?

options.A: Viruses can reproduce independently on agar plates
options.B: Viruses are acellular and need a host to multiply
options.C: Viruses possess both DNA and RNA simultaneously
options.D: Viruses have thick peptidoglycan cell walls

explanation: Viruses lack cellular machinery of their own and must infect host cells to replicate. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is the protein coat that encloses viral genetic material called?

options.A: Peptidoglycan
options.B: Plasmid
options.C: Capsid
options.D: Flagellum

explanation: The capsid is the protective protein shell that surrounds the viral nucleic acid. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h3)

question: How do bacteria primarily reproduce in the human body?

options.A: Sexual conjugation
options.B: Host cell hijacking
options.C: Spore germination
options.D: Binary fission

explanation: Bacteria multiply asexually by dividing into two equal halves through binary fission. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h3)

question: What are thread-like structures of multicellular molds called?

options.A: Hyphae
options.B: Capsules
options.C: Spore
options.D: Plasmids

explanation: Molds grow as branching, thread-like filaments known collectively as hyphae. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h4)

question: What distinguishes the definitive host of a parasite?

options.A: The parasite only reproduces asexually in this host
options.B: The definitive host harbors the adult or sexual stage
options.C: The definitive host never shows clinical symptoms of infection
options.D: The intermediate host is always larger than the definitive host

explanation: Sexual maturity and reproduction of the parasite occur within the definitive host. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which process eliminates all microbial life including bacterial spores?

options.A: Sterilization
options.B: Antisepsis
options.C: Disinfection
options.D: Sanitization

explanation: Sterilization is the highest level of cleaning and destroys every form of microbial life. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h5)

question: When should a nurse choose an antiseptic rather than a disinfectant?

options.A: When wiping down a metal examination table
options.B: When washing contaminated bed linens
options.C: When sterilizing surgical steel forceps
options.D: When cleaning unbroken skin prior to an injection

explanation: Antiseptics are formulated specifically for application on living tissue like skin to reduce microbes. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h5)

question: What test determines which antibiotics will kill an isolated bacterial pathogen?

options.A: Direct microscopy
options.B: Serology screening
options.C: Sensitivity testing
options.D: Gram staining

explanation: Antimicrobial sensitivity testing shows which drugs are effective against a specific cultured organism. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the main difference between microbial colonization and a true infection?

options.A: Colonization only occurs on sterile internal body organs
options.B: Colonization involves organism presence without tissue damage or symptoms
options.C: Infection never causes fever or laboratory abnormalities
options.D: Colonization always requires immediate intravenous antibiotic therapy

explanation: Colonizers live on or in the host without causing disease or triggering active tissue destruction. [learn more](GST114_U1_T1#GST114_U1_T1_h6)

question: What does microbiology study?

options.A: Geological rock formations
options.B: Microscopic organisms
options.C: Large plant structures
options.D: Human skeletal systems

explanation: Microbiology specifically focuses on living things and agents that are too small to see without magnification. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why did ancient healers fail to cure infectious diseases effectively?

options.A: They used herbs that neutralized all medicines
options.B: They lacked knowledge of unseen microbes
options.C: They only treated wealthy members of society
options.D: They refused to use clean water supplies

explanation: Without optical instruments, early societies had no way to identify bacteria or viruses as the root cause of infections. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h1)

question: What does the theory of spontaneous generation state?

options.A: Boiling liquids destroys all organic matter
options.B: Diseases are spread through contaminated water
options.C: Life arises from non-living matter
options.D: Microbes only come from other microbes

explanation: Spontaneous generation was the mistaken belief that living organisms could form out of inanimate substances. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h2)

question: What was the main purpose of Louis Pasteur using swan-neck flasks?

options.A: To speed up the evaporation of broth
options.B: To prevent pressure from breaking the glass
options.C: To trap dust while letting air enter
options.D: To heat the liquid to extreme temperatures

explanation: The curved neck allowed air in but trapped airborne particles and microbes, keeping the broth sterile. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h2)

question: Who was the first person to observe bacteria using a simple microscope?

options.A: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
options.B: Joseph Lister
options.C: Robert Koch
options.D: Louis Pasteur

explanation: Leeuwenhoek handcrafted powerful single-lens microscopes and recorded the first descriptions of microorganisms. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h3)

question: How do electron microscopes differ from light microscopes?

options.A: They are small enough to carry in a pocket
options.B: They rely on natural sunlight for illumination
options.C: They produce images in full color automatically
options.D: They use electron beams instead of light

explanation: Using electrons allows for much higher resolution, making it possible to see tiny viruses that light microscopes miss. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary focus of the germ theory of disease?

options.A: Clean air prevents all bacterial growth
options.B: Specific microbes cause specific illnesses
options.C: Boiling water removes toxic minerals
options.D: Chemicals can cure any viral infection

explanation: The germ theory replaced older miasma beliefs by proving individual pathogens drive specific diseases. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why must a pathogen be grown in pure culture during Koch's steps?

options.A: To make the bacteria multiply faster
options.B: To destroy any viral particles present
options.C: To change the color of the nutrient agar
options.D: To ensure only one germ is tested

explanation: A pure culture ensures that any symptoms in the test animal come from one specific organism and nothing else. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h4)

question: What disease did Edward Jenner use to protect people against smallpox?

options.A: Measles
options.B: Chickenpox
options.C: Rabies
options.D: Cowpox

explanation: Jenner used milder cowpox lesions to stimulate immunity against the deadly smallpox virus. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h5)

question: How was penicillin discovered by Alexander Fleming?

options.A: Chemicals in soil cured infected laboratory mice
options.B: A mold contaminant inhibited bacterial growth
options.C: He boiled sewage water until crystals formed
options.D: He tested thousands of plant roots in a lab

explanation: Fleming noticed a fungal spore drifted onto his culture plate and created a clear zone where bacteria could not grow. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is handwashing before and after patient care critical in a Nigerian ward?

options.A: It removes unpleasant odors from the skin
options.B: It satisfies hospital accreditation rules
options.C: It prevents skin oils from staining linens
options.D: It breaks the chain of microbial transmission

explanation: Mechanical removal of transient flora through hand hygiene stops pathogens from spreading between patients. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is a major nursing responsibility related to antibiotic therapy?

options.A: Stopping medication as soon as fever drops
options.B: Administering full courses to prevent resistance
options.C: Diluting syrups with water for faster action
options.D: Prescribing stronger drugs for viral colds

explanation: Completing prescribed antibiotic regimens ensures all target pathogens are eliminated, preventing drug-resistant strains. [learn more](GST114_U1_T2#GST114_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary focus of microbiology in nursing?

options.A: Calculating precise drug dosages for pediatric patients
options.B: Assessing nutritional needs in surgical recovery
options.C: Studying tiny organisms invisible to the naked eye
options.D: Managing hospital financial records and budgets

explanation: Microbiology specifically investigates microorganisms like bacteria and viruses that cannot be seen without magnification. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why must a nurse view routine clinical procedures through a microbiological lens?

options.A: To ensure faster discharge times for routine surgical cases
options.B: To reduce the physical effort required during long ward shifts
options.C: To comply strictly with hospital billing and insurance policies
options.D: To prevent the unintentional transfer of harmful microbes to patients

explanation: Understanding where microbes live and how they spread guides nurses to perform procedures safely and stop cross-infection. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h1)

question: What term describes the natural habitat where a pathogen lives and multiplies?

options.A: Infectious vector
options.B: Reservoir
options.C: Portal of entry
options.D: Susceptible host

explanation: A reservoir provides a place for microorganisms to live, thrive, and reproduce before infecting a host. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: Hand hygiene stops the spread of infection by interrupting which part of the chain?

options.A: Infectious agent mutation
options.B: Portal of exit creation
options.C: Mode of transmission
options.D: Susceptible host age

explanation: Washing hands removes pathogens from the hands, preventing them from traveling between patients and surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of medical asepsis?

options.A: Reducing the overall number of disease-causing microorganisms
options.B: Eliminating every single bacterial spore on an instrument
options.C: Destroying viral particles using high-pressure steam autoclaves
options.D: Sterilizing the entire operating room air ventilation system

explanation: Medical asepsis focuses on decreasing microbial load and stopping transmission, unlike surgical asepsis which seeks total eradication. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: Which procedure requires strict adherence to surgical asepsis rather than medical asepsis?

options.A: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
options.B: Administering an oral antibiotic tablet
options.C: Measuring vital signs in a general outpatient clinic
options.D: Assisting a stable patient with a bed bath

explanation: Urinary catheterization enters a sterile body cavity, requiring complete elimination of all microbes to prevent infection. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h3)

question: What causes antimicrobial resistance to develop rapidly in clinical settings?

options.A: Storing vaccines at incorrect refrigerator temperatures
options.B: Routine handwashing with standard hospital soap
options.C: Misuse and overuse of prescribed antimicrobial medications
options.D: Collecting blood samples using expired specimen tubes

explanation: When drugs are used improperly, resilient microbes survive, adapt, and multiply, rendering standard treatments ineffective. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: A patient wants to stop taking antibiotics after three days because fever symptoms have disappeared. What is the nurse's best response?

options.A: Agree and advise keeping the remaining pills for the next illness
options.B: Explain that stopping early allows surviving resistant bacteria to multiply
options.C: Contact the doctor immediately to request a switch to liquid syrup
options.D: Suggest doubling the dose to finish the treatment pack much faster

explanation: Patients must finish the full prescription to eradicate all pathogens, preventing the survival of drug-resistant mutants. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h4)

question: When should blood cultures be drawn in relation to starting antimicrobial therapy?

options.A: At any time during the hospital admission process
options.B: Before administering the prescribed antimicrobial drugs
options.C: Only after the patient completes the full drug course
options.D: Two hours after the first intravenous dose is given

explanation: Starting antimicrobials before collection can kill the pathogens in the vial, resulting in a false-negative laboratory report. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why is a midstream urine sample required instead of a routine collection?

options.A: To flush out contaminating bacteria residing near the urethral opening
options.B: To ensure the laboratory receives a much larger volume of fluid
options.C: To prevent the chemical reagents from reacting with container walls
options.D: To capture only the bacteria living inside the urinary bladder

explanation: The initial urine stream washes away normal skin flora, ensuring the sample reflects actual infection inside the urinary tract. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h5)

question: What type of immunity is gained when an infant receives maternal antibodies across the placenta?

options.A: Artificial active immunity
options.B: Natural passive immunity
options.C: Active acquired immunity
options.D: Innate cellular immunity

explanation: Passing antibodies naturally from mother to child provides immediate, temporary protection without the infant's immune system mounting a response. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: How do vaccines protect a community against infectious disease outbreaks?

options.A: By changing the genetic makeup of human cells to resist toxins
options.B: By killing all environmental bacteria present in drinking water supplies
options.C: By building herd immunity and reducing the number of susceptible hosts
options.D: By curing individuals who are already experiencing severe acute symptoms

explanation: High vaccination rates lower the pool of vulnerable people, stopping the chain of transmission and protecting unvaccinated individuals. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which complication can occur if a localized wound infection is left untreated?

options.A: Permanent stabilization of local blood pressure
options.B: Immediate regeneration of normal skin pigmentation
options.C: Rapid closure of the wound edges by scar tissue
options.D: Systemic sepsis spreading through the bloodstream

explanation: Pathogens multiplying in a localized wound can invade deeper tissues and enter circulation, causing life-threatening systemic infection. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why must nurses understand the specific mechanisms of action of antibacterial drugs?

options.A: To anticipate potential side effects and evaluate treatment effectiveness
options.B: To diagnose underlying viral infections without laboratory support
options.C: To compound raw chemical powders into injectable solutions safely
options.D: To calculate hospital expenditure on surgical dressings and sutures

explanation: Knowing how drugs target microbial cell walls or proteins helps nurses monitor patient recovery and identify adverse reactions early. [learn more](GST114_U1_T3#GST114_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of microbial taxonomy in healthcare?

options.A: To determine the exact cost of laboratory tests
options.B: To destroy harmful pathogens on hospital surfaces
options.C: To organize and identify microorganisms systematically
options.D: To calculate the growth rate of human cells

explanation: Taxonomy gives healthcare workers a standardized system to classify and name microorganisms for clear communication. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which part of the scientific name *Staphylococcus aureus* represents the genus?

options.A: Neither word
options.B: Both words combined
options.C: Staphylococcus
options.D: aureus

explanation: In binomial nomenclature, the first capitalized word always designates the genus, while the second indicates the species. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the highest and broadest rank in biological classification?

options.A: Family
options.B: Phylum
options.C: Species
options.D: Domain

explanation: The domain sits at the very top of the taxonomic hierarchy, dividing life into major cellular categories. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h2)

question: The suffix *-aceae* at the end of a microbial name typically indicates which taxonomic rank?

options.A: Domain
options.B: Species
options.C: Family
options.D: Strain

question: What color do Gram-negative bacteria appear after the complete Gram staining procedure?

options.A: Dark purple
options.B: Clear or colorless

question: A laboratory report describes spherical bacteria clustered together like grapes. What term describes this arrangement?

options.A: Streptococci
options.B: Staphylococci
options.C: Diplobacilli
options.D: Spirilla

question: What protective protein coat surrounds the viral genetic material?

options.A: Peptidoglycan
options.B: Lipopolysaccharide
options.C: Mycolic acid
options.D: Capsid

explanation: The capsid is the protein shell that encases and protects the viral nucleic acid genome. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h4)

question: A patient is diagnosed with an infection caused by a virus possessing an outer lipid bilayer. What is this outer layer called?

options.A: Cell wall
options.B: Envelope
options.C: Nucleoid
options.D: Capsomere

question: Which key cellular feature distinguishes fungi and parasites from bacteria?

options.A: Absence of a cell membrane
options.B: Presence of a true nucleus
options.C: Ability to reproduce without nutrients
options.D: Presence of peptidoglycan walls

explanation: Fungi and parasites are eukaryotic organisms characterized by true membrane-bound nuclei and organelles. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h5)

question: What type of organism is *Plasmodium*, the causative agent of malaria?

options.A: Fungus
options.B: Virus
options.C: Protozoan
options.D: Bacterium

question: What is the main advantage of molecular methods over traditional microbial staining?

options.A: Higher accuracy based on genetic blueprints
options.B: Elimination of the need for any laboratory equipment
options.C: Lower cost for every routine test
options.D: Ability to grow viruses on plain nutrient agar

question: Which laboratory technology identifies microbes by analyzing their unique protein mass fingerprints?

options.A: Wet mount preparation
options.B: Simple Gram staining
options.C: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry
options.D: Acid-fast microscopy

explanation: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry rapidly identifies microorganisms by matching their unique cellular protein profiles against a reference database. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h6)

question: A laboratory report identifies a patient's wound infection as a Gram-negative bacillus. How does this information assist nursing care?

options.A: It proves the patient has a viral respiratory illness
options.B: It shows that the infection will resolve without medical intervention
options.C: It indicates that no isolation precautions are ever required
options.D: It guides appropriate infection control and targeted antibiotic therapy

explanation: Knowing the specific bacterial classification helps the healthcare team select effective medications and implement proper barrier nursing. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why must nurses understand basic microbial classification during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: To manufacture vaccines directly at the bedside
options.B: To apply correct isolation and barrier precautions effectively
options.C: To perform advanced gene sequencing in hospital rooms
options.D: To rewrite hospital administrative policies

explanation: Understanding how pathogens are categorized helps nurses anticipate transmission routes and apply appropriate containment measures. [learn more](GST114_U1_T4#GST114_U1_T4_h7)

question: How many distinct links make up the standard chain of infection?

options.A: Six links
options.B: Eight links
options.C: Four links
options.D: Ten links

explanation: The chain of infection is composed of six sequential links, starting with the infectious agent and ending with a susceptible host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h1)

question: What happens to an infection cycle if a nurse successfully blocks the portal of entry?

options.A: The pathogen multiplies faster
options.B: The reservoir changes its location
options.C: The host becomes immediately immune
options.D: The chain of infection is broken

question: What term describes a human reservoir who harbors a pathogen without showing any symptoms?

options.A: A primary vector
options.B: An active host
options.C: A resistant source
options.D: A passive carrier

explanation: Asymptomatic or passive carriers harbor and shed infectious agents without experiencing clinical illness themselves. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which of these represents an environmental reservoir for tetanus spores?

options.A: Ordinary garden soil
options.B: Infected mosquito saliva
options.C: Stagnant tap water
options.D: Unwashed hospital linens

explanation: Clostridium tetani spores reside naturally in soil and enter the body through breaks in the skin. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is an inanimate object that transfers infectious agents between patients called?

options.A: A vector
options.B: A fomite
options.C: A droplet nucleus
options.D: A reservoir

explanation: Fomites are non-living items like instruments or furniture that passively carry and transfer pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which scenario is an example of vector-borne transmission?

options.A: Contracting malaria from a mosquito bite
options.B: Sharing a contaminated pen with a colleague
options.C: Inhaling tuberculosis bacteria from room air
options.D: Drinking contaminated water during an outbreak

explanation: Vectors are living organisms, such as mosquitoes, that carry pathogens from one host to another. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h3)

question: Which portal of entry is most commonly bypassed by an intravenous cannula?

options.A: The mucous membranes
options.B: The gastrointestinal lining
options.C: The respiratory tract
options.D: The skin barrier

question: How do enteric pathogens typically leave the human body?

options.A: Through skin lesions
options.B: Through respiratory sputum
options.C: Through stool and vomit
options.D: Through sweat secretions

explanation: Gastrointestinal pathogens exit the infected host primarily through fecal matter and vomitus. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h4)

question: What term describes the natural decrease in immune function that occurs with advanced age?

options.A: Immunosenescence
options.B: Seroconversion
options.C: Hypersensitivity
options.D: Immunization

explanation: Immunosenescence refers to the gradual deterioration of the immune system brought on by natural aging. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: A patient with severe protein malnutrition is admitted to the ward. What is their primary infection risk?

options.A: They have increased susceptibility to invading pathogens
options.B: They will develop rapid antibiotic resistance
options.C: They will automatically trigger airborne isolation needs
options.D: They act as a permanent environmental reservoir

explanation: Poor nutrition compromises immune cell function, leaving the host highly susceptible to infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h5)

question: During which stage of an infection does a patient experience vague, non-specific symptoms like fatigue?

options.A: The prodromal stage
options.B: The incubation period
options.C: The illness stage
options.D: The convalescent stage

explanation: The prodromal stage features early, generalized signs before classic disease-specific symptoms appear. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: What defines the incubation period of an infectious disease?

options.A: The timeframe when antibiotics completely eliminate the microbe
options.B: The duration when specific rashes and fevers are peaking
options.C: The recovery phase where body tissues are finally repaired
options.D: The time from pathogen entry until first symptoms appear

explanation: Incubation is the silent phase between exposure and the onset of any clinical signs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is recognized as the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infections?

options.A: Isolating every surgical patient
options.B: Wearing sterile gowns
options.C: Administering daily antibiotics
options.D: Proper hand hygiene

explanation: Frequent and correct hand hygiene removes transient flora and stops cross-contamination between patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)

question: Which personal protective equipment is required for caring for a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: A fitted N95 respirator
options.B: A standard surgical mask
options.C: A disposable plastic apron
options.D: Sterile latex gloves only

explanation: Airborne pathogens like tuberculosis require specialized respiratory protection such as an N95 mask. [learn more](GST114_U2_T1#GST114_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of disinfection in a healthcare facility?

options.A: To remove all living bacterial spores completely
options.B: To sterilize surgical instruments before invasive procedures
options.C: To reduce pathogens on inanimate objects to safe levels
options.D: To destroy all microorganisms on living human skin

explanation: Disinfection targets inanimate surfaces to lower pathogen counts safely, as it rarely eliminates all bacterial spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h1)

question: How does a bacteriostatic agent differ from a bactericidal agent?

options.A: Bacteriostatic agents are chemical while bactericidal agents are physical
options.B: Bacteriostatic agents work on living tissue while bactericidal work on surfaces
options.C: Bacteriostatic agents stop bacterial growth while bactericidal agents kill them
options.D: Bacteriostatic agents destroy spores while bactericidal destroy vegetative cells

explanation: Static agents halt reproduction without killing, whereas cidal agents actively destroy the microorganisms. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which process achieves the complete elimination of all microbial life including spores?

options.A: Disinfection
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Decontamination
options.D: Antisepsis

explanation: Sterilization destroys every form of microbial life, making it the most thorough level of germ removal. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why should chemical disinfectants NOT be used as skin antiseptics?

options.A: They destroy living human tissue and delay healing
options.B: They leave a greasy residue that attracts more dirt
options.C: They are completely ineffective against bacteria on skin
options.D: They only work when exposed to high atmospheric pressure

explanation: Disinfectants are formulated for inanimate objects and are too toxic for living cellular structures. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h2)

question: Which level of disinfection is required for semi-critical items like endoscopes?

options.A: Standard decontamination
options.B: High-level disinfection
options.C: Intermediate disinfection
options.D: Low-level disinfection

explanation: Semi-critical items touch mucous membranes and require high-level disinfection to eliminate nearly all pathogens except some spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h3)

question: A nurse needs to disinfect a stethoscope contaminated with dried blood. Which level of disinfection is necessary?

options.A: Intermediate-level disinfection
options.B: Low-level disinfection
options.C: High-level disinfection
options.D: Complete steam sterilization

explanation: Presence of blood on non-critical items requires intermediate-level disinfection to ensure hepatitis and tuberculosis agents are inactivated. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which chemical agent is most commonly utilized for cleaning blood spills on surfaces?

options.A: Glutaraldehyde solution
options.B: Hydrogen peroxide
options.C: Sodium hypochlorite
options.D: Isopropyl alcohol

explanation: Sodium hypochlorite (chlorine bleach) is the standard, cost-effective agent for inactivating bloodborne pathogens on environmental surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is a major clinical limitation of using alcohol as a surface disinfectant?

options.A: It reacts violently when mixed with ordinary tap water
options.B: It corrodes stainless steel instruments over time
options.C: It leaves a sticky residue that attracts airborne dust
options.D: It evaporates too quickly to maintain required contact time

explanation: Alcohols dry rapidly, which can prevent them from staying wet long enough to kill resilient microbes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h4)

question: Why is pre-cleaning a heavily soiled instrument mandatory before chemical disinfection?

options.A: Soap increases the room temperature for faster chemical action
options.B: Dried dirt makes the equipment too heavy to lift safely
options.C: Organic matter inactivates the disinfectant and blocks contact
options.D: Washing prevents the metal from changing its color

explanation: Blood and protein residues shield microbes and absorb active chemicals, neutralizing the disinfectant's power. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h5)

question: What happens when a disinfectant is wiped off a surface prematurely?

options.A: The required contact time is not met, causing failure
options.B: The chemical reaction speeds up due to friction
options.C: The disinfectant leaves a protective glossy coating
options.D: The surface becomes instantly sterile

explanation: Chemicals need a specific duration of continuous wet contact to destroy microbial cell walls. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h5)

question: How are medical items that enter the vascular system or sterile tissues classified?

options.A: Environmental items
options.B: Non-critical items
options.C: Critical items
options.D: Semi-critical items

explanation: Critical items bypass natural body barriers, carrying a high infection risk and requiring absolute sterility. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h6)

question: A blood pressure cuff used on an adult patient with intact skin falls under which Spaulding category?

options.A: Sterilization-dependent
options.B: Critical
options.C: Non-critical
options.D: Semi-critical

explanation: Since the cuff only contacts unbroken skin, it is a non-critical device needing basic disinfection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the correct physical direction for cleaning ward surfaces and patient units?

options.A: From the cleanest area toward the dirtiest area
options.B: From the center of the room outward to the walls
options.C: Randomly across all surfaces until they appear dry
options.D: From the dirtiest area toward the cleanest area

explanation: Moving from clean to dirty zones prevents spreading heavy microbial loads onto cleaner, low-risk surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h7)

question: Which items in a patient room are classified as high-touch surfaces needing frequent disinfection?

options.A: Underneath heavy bedside lockers
options.B: Bed rails and call buttons
options.C: Ceiling tiles and upper wall corners
options.D: Window glass frames and curtains

explanation: Bed rails and call buttons are frequently handled by hands, making them primary vectors for germ transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h7)

question: What dangerous hazard occurs when bleach is mixed with an acid or ammonia?

options.A: It creates an explosion hazard from excess heat
options.B: It turns the solution into a harmless clear gel
options.C: It generates lethal and toxic chemical gases
options.D: It neutralizes the cleaning power completely

explanation: Mixing cleaning chemicals creates dangerous toxic fumes that can severely damage the respiratory tract. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h8)

question: Why must nurses wear utility gloves and eye protection when handling concentrated disinfectants?

options.A: To prevent chemical burns, splashes, and tissue irritation
options.B: To prevent fingerprints on polished glass surfaces
options.C: To keep hands warm during cold morning ward rounds
options.D: To maintain sterile fields during major surgical operations

explanation: Concentrated germicides are corrosive and cause severe damage if they contact skin or mucous membranes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T10#GST114_U2_T10_h8)

question: What does complete sterilization successfully destroy that disinfection usually misses?

options.A: Fungal hyphae
options.B: Bacterial endospores
options.C: Lipid-coated viruses
options.D: Vegetative bacteria

explanation: Endospores possess thick, protective coats that resist standard disinfectants but are destroyed during proper sterilization. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h1)

question: A medical instrument is labeled as sterile. What condition must be true for this label to be accurate?

options.A: It carries only harmless bacteria that cannot cause disease.
options.B: It has been washed thoroughly with ordinary soap and water.
options.C: It is completely free of all living microorganisms and spores.
options.D: It has been wiped down with a standard antiseptic solution.

explanation: Sterility is an absolute state meaning zero viable microorganisms or resistant spores remain on the item. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which infection control process is safe and appropriate to apply directly to living human skin?

options.A: High-level disinfection
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Antisepsis
options.D: Incineration

explanation: Antiseptics are formulated specifically to reduce microbial load on skin and living tissues without causing severe chemical burns. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h2)

question: A nurse needs to prepare a patient's abdomen before an exploratory laparotomy. Which process should be performed?

options.A: Desiccation
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Pasteurization
options.D: Antisepsis

explanation: Skin preparation requires an antiseptic agent because living tissue cannot undergo physical sterilization methods like autoclaving. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the standard temperature and pressure used in a hospital autoclave for effective steam sterilization?

options.A: 100°C at 5 psi
options.B: 121°C at 15 psi
options.C: 72°C at atmospheric pressure
options.D: 160°C at 30 psi

explanation: Operating at 121°C with 15 pounds of pressure allows steam to penetrate wrapped packs and destroy resilient spores efficiently. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h3)

question: Why is dry heat sterilization preferred over moist heat for sharp surgical instruments made of carbon steel?

options.A: Moist heat causes moisture accumulation that leads to rust and blunts sharp edges.
options.B: Dry heat destroys endospores in a fraction of the time required by steam.
options.C: Dry heat utilizes electricity instead of expensive pressurized water systems.
options.D: Autoclaves are physically unable to accommodate metal surgical scissors.

explanation: Water vapor and condensation in steam autoclaves can corrode delicate carbon steel instruments, making dry heat ovens a better choice. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h3)

question: What critical post-processing step is required for medical equipment sterilized using ethylene oxide gas?

options.A: Immediate rinsing in sterile normal saline
options.B: Aeration to remove toxic gas residues
options.C: Exposure to ultraviolet germicidal irradiation
options.D: Submersion in a cold glutaraldehyde bath

explanation: Ethylene oxide is a toxic and mutagenic chemical, so items must undergo controlled aeration to off-gas residual vapors safely. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h4)

question: When must a nurse choose a chemical sterilant over a steam autoclave?

options.A: When the items being processed are simple glass reagent bottles
options.B: When surgical trays contain large volumes of heavy metallic instruments
options.C: When the hospital has an unlimited supply of electricity but no water
options.D: When the medical equipment is sensitive to high heat and moisture

explanation: Heat-sensitive plastics, lenses, and electronic components would melt or break down inside a steam autoclave. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the standard pore size of a membrane filter used to remove bacteria from heat-sensitive liquids?

options.A: 50 nanometers
options.B: 0.22 micrometers
options.C: 2.0 millimeters
options.D: 10 micrometers

explanation: A 0.22-micrometer pore size is small enough to retain virtually all bacteria and fungi while allowing sterile liquid to pass through. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h5)

question: Why is ionizing radiation primarily restricted to large-scale industrial manufacturing rather than routine ward use?

options.A: It takes up to seventy-two hours to complete a single sterilization cycle.
options.B: It requires massive radiation shielding facilities and specialized handling equipment.
options.C: It leaves radioactive particles behind on every single treated instrument.
options.D: It is completely ineffective against bacterial endospores and fungal spores.

explanation: Gamma irradiators and electron beam accelerators demand heavy concrete bunkers and strict regulatory safety controls absent in standard hospitals. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which monitoring indicator provides the most definitive proof that microbial spores were actually destroyed?

options.A: Digital cycle printouts
options.B: Chemical indicator tape
options.C: Biological indicators
options.D: Mechanical pressure gauges

explanation: Biological indicators test actual resistance by challenging the cycle with living, highly resilient bacterial spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h6)

question: What is the specific purpose of placing chemical indicator tape on the outside of a wrapped instrument tray?

options.A: To provide visual verification that the pack has been exposed to a sterilization process
options.B: To seal the wrapping paper so tightly that ambient room air cannot enter the tray
options.C: To prove conclusively that every single bacterial endospore inside the pack is dead
options.D: To measure the exact internal temperature reached at the core of the heavy metal instruments

explanation: Color changes on chemical tape indicate processing has occurred, though they do not guarantee that every parameter was maintained for the full duration. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h6)

question: Why is a newly removed autoclave pack with damp wrapping paper considered contaminated?

options.A: Damp wrappers cause chemical indicators to permanently revert to their original color.
options.B: Moisture allows microorganisms to wick through the porous paper barrier from the outside.
options.C: Moisture prevents the surgical metal inside from cooling down quickly enough.
options.D: Wet paper indicates that the machine reached a temperature higher than 150°C.

explanation: Water droplets create capillary pathways that let ambient bacteria cross the sterile barrier, breaking package integrity. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h7)

question: A nurse notices that an instrument tray has a small tear in its paper wrapper just before a surgical procedure. What action should be taken?

options.A: Reject the tray and obtain a newly sterilized replacement pack.
options.B: Cover the tear with ordinary adhesive plaster and proceed.
options.C: Use the instruments immediately before ambient air contaminates them.
options.D: Spray the outside of the torn wrapper with a surface antiseptic.

explanation: A torn wrapper compromises the sterile barrier, meaning the contents are no longer considered sterile and must be reprocessed or replaced. [learn more](GST114_U2_T11#GST114_U2_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of asepsis in healthcare?

options.A: The reduction of visible dust on surfaces
options.B: The chemical destruction of skin tissues
options.C: The total absence of disease-producing microorganisms
options.D: The complete elimination of all water sources

explanation: Asepsis literally means free from infection or contaminating microorganisms. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h1)

question: Hospital-acquired infections are also commonly referred to by what name?

options.A: Congenital disorders
options.B: Zoonotic diseases
options.C: Nosocomial infections
options.D: Idiopathic conditions

explanation: Infections that originate or develop within a hospital or healthcare facility are termed nosocomial infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h1)

question: Medical asepsis is best described by which term?

options.A: Surgical protocol
options.B: Isolation barrier
options.C: Sterile technique
options.D: Clean technique

explanation: Medical asepsis involves practices that reduce the number and transfer of pathogens, commonly known as clean technique. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h2)

question: When is surgical asepsis strictly required during routine nursing tasks?

options.A: Administering oral capsule medications
options.B: Assisting a client with ambulation
options.C: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
options.D: Feeding a patient with dysphagia

explanation: Catheter insertion enters a sterile body cavity, requiring full surgical asepsis to prevent introducing bacteria. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h2)

question: An environment where a pathogen can live and multiply is called what?

options.A: A susceptible host
options.B: A transmission vehicle
options.C: A portal of entry
options.D: A reservoir

explanation: A reservoir provides a suitable habitat for microorganisms to grow, multiply, and survive. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h3)

question: Handwashing primarily breaks which link in the chain of infection?

options.A: Mode of transmission
options.B: Infectious agent
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Portal of exit

explanation: Washing hands removes transient microbes, preventing them from transferring from one surface or person to another. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h3)

question: What is the single most effective way to prevent the spread of infections?

options.A: Administering prophylactic antibiotics
options.B: Proper hand hygiene
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns
options.D: Using disposable trays

explanation: Frequent and proper handwashing or sanitizing removes pathogens before they can spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h4)

question: Standard precautions must be used for which category of hospital patients?

options.A: All patients in the healthcare setting
options.B: Only patients with confirmed tuberculosis
options.C: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.D: Individuals with diagnosed blood infections

explanation: Standard precautions apply universally to care for every patient to minimize unseen transmission risks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h4)

question: What part of a sterile drape is considered contaminated by default?

options.A: The exact center of the field
options.B: The upper right quadrant only
options.C: The bottom surface facing the tray
options.D: The outer one-inch border

explanation: The outer edge touches unsterile surfaces during setup, making the outer one-inch margin contaminated. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why does moisture cause a sterile field to become contaminated?

options.A: Water changes the chemical pH of sterile instruments
options.B: It allows bacteria to move through the barrier via capillary action
options.C: Moisture attracts dust particles from the room ventilation
options.D: Wet packages instantly dissolve surgical steel

explanation: Liquid creates a bridge that pulls microorganisms through porous sterile wrappers from non-sterile surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h5)

question: Which process completely eliminates all microbial life, including bacterial spores?

options.A: Sterilization
options.B: Cleaning
options.C: Sanitization
options.D: Disinfection

explanation: Sterilization is the only process that destroys every form of microbial life, including tough spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of cleaning instruments before disinfection or sterilization?

options.A: To cool down items that were heated in storage
options.B: To remove organic material that can block germicidal action
options.C: To polish the stainless steel surfaces for better grip
options.D: To ensure the equipment smells clean for patients

explanation: Blood, tissue, and debris protect microorganisms from disinfectants, so cleaning must happen first. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h6)

question: What should a nurse do immediately if a break in sterile technique occurs?

options.A: Ask the patient if they noticed any dirty tools
options.B: Take corrective action and replace the contaminated item
options.C: Wait until the procedure ends to report the incident
options.D: Ignore it if the item only touched a clean glove

explanation: Integrity of the sterile field must be maintained; contaminated items must be replaced immediately. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h7)

question: How does the nurse directly protect vulnerable patients through asepsis?

options.A: By locking room doors to keep visitors away permanently
options.B: By consistently practicing proper hand hygiene and barrier techniques
options.C: By prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics to every new admission
options.D: By wiping down walls with bleach solution hourly

explanation: Consistent application of aseptic habits stops pathogens from reaching susceptible patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T12#GST114_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of asepsis in clinical practice?

options.A: The absence of disease-producing microorganisms
options.B: The complete absence of all living organisms
options.C: The reduction of visible dirt on instruments
options.D: The chemical disinfection of intact skin

explanation: Asepsis specifically targets pathogenic germs to prevent them from entering vulnerable tissues and causing disease. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why is strict adherence to infection control vital in Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: It eliminates the need for expensive antibiotic therapy
options.B: It reduces the total number of hospital staff required
options.C: It guarantees complete immunity against airborne viruses
options.D: It prevents prolonged hospital stays from surgical infections

explanation: Controlling microbial contamination directly reduces post-operative complications that keep patients hospitalized longer. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which practice is also known as clean technique?

options.A: Medical asepsis
options.B: Barrier nursing
options.C: Surgical asepsis
options.D: Terminal sterilization

explanation: Medical asepsis focuses on reducing the overall number of disease-causing germs rather than achieving complete sterility. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h2)

question: A nurse is preparing to insert an indwelling urinary catheter. Which technique must be used?

options.A: Standard precautions using clean disposable gloves only
options.B: Medical asepsis to protect surrounding bed linen
options.C: Routine disinfection without the use of barriers
options.D: Surgical asepsis to prevent introducing germs into the bladder

explanation: Inserting a catheter into the sterile bladder requires surgical asepsis to avoid causing a urinary tract infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of positive pressure ventilation in the operating theatre?

options.A: To dry surgical instruments quickly after washing
options.B: To circulate humidified oxygen throughout the room
options.C: To push air outward and prevent outside contaminants from entering
options.D: To cool down the surgical team under heavy gowns

explanation: Positive pressure forces air from the clean room toward less clean corridors, protecting the sterile field from airborne dust and microbes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which operating theatre zone requires full surgical attire and masks?

options.A: Unrestricted zone
options.B: General waiting zone
options.C: Restricted zone
options.D: Semi-restricted zone

explanation: The restricted zone contains the actual operating rooms where the highest level of sterility must be maintained. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h3)

question: A nurse touches a sterile wrapper's outer edge while opening a pack. What should be done?

options.A: Consider the item contaminated and discard it
options.B: Ask the surgeon for permission to use it
options.C: Use the item anyway if it looks clean
options.D: Wipe the edge with alcohol and proceed

explanation: Any doubt regarding sterility means the item must be treated as contaminated to safeguard the patient. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h4)

question: The edges of a sterile package are considered what once opened?

options.A: Sterile
options.B: Self-cleaning
options.C: Non-sterile
options.D: Protected

explanation: The outer perimeter of any sterile wrapper touches the unsterile environment during opening, rendering its edges non-sterile. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h4)

question: In which direction should water flow during a surgical hand scrub?

options.A: From fingertips down to the elbows
options.B: From elbows down to the fingertips
options.C: Directly onto the palms and wrists
options.D: From forearms outward to the sides

explanation: Water must flow downward from the cleanest area, the fingertips, toward the elbows to prevent dirty water from contaminating washed skin. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h5)

question: Why must a scrubbed nurse keep their hands higher than their elbows?

options.A: To improve blood circulation in the fingers during long surgeries
options.B: To make it easier to see the surgical instruments
options.C: To prevent water from running back down from the arms onto clean hands
options.D: To ensure the sterile gown sleeves stay securely tied

explanation: Keeping hands elevated ensures that any residual moisture flows away from the hands toward the unwashed upper arms. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h5)

question: What is the primary mechanism of action in an autoclave?

options.A: Ultraviolet light exposure
options.B: Pressurized steam
options.C: Chemical gas immersion
options.D: Dry heat radiation

explanation: Autoclaves use moist heat under pressure to effectively destroy all microorganisms and spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h6)

question: Why are biological spore tests used in instrument sterilization?

options.A: To prove that the autoclave successfully killed resistant test spores
options.B: To measure the exact weight of the surgical tray
options.C: To check if the instrument packaging is waterproof
options.D: To clean dried blood off complex metal hinges

explanation: Biological indicators contain highly resistant spores, confirming the sterilization cycle's effectiveness when they fail to grow after processing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h6)

question: A circulating nurse needs to drop a sterile item onto the sterile table. What action is required?

options.A: Reach across the table and place it gently down
options.B: Throw the item from a distance onto the center
options.C: Transfer the item carefully from a safe distance without touching the field
options.D: Ask an unscrubbed porter to hand it over

explanation: Unscrubbed personnel must maintain a safe distance and drop items onto the sterile field without reaching across it. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h7)

question: What is the main risk of turning your back on a sterile field?

options.A: Your sterile gown will automatically tear
options.B: The scrub nurse will become distracted
options.C: You cannot see if unsterile clothing accidentally brushes against it
options.D: The surgical lights will overheat your back

explanation: Unseen contamination can easily occur behind a person, making it vital to always face the sterile field. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h7)

question: Which nurse works directly within the sterile field during an operation?

options.A: The scrub nurse
options.B: The circulating nurse
options.C: The ward recovery nurse
options.D: The triage nurse

explanation: The scrub nurse wears sterile garb and assists the surgeon directly at the operative site. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h8)

question: What is a primary responsibility of the circulating nurse regarding asepsis?

options.A: Handing sterile instruments directly to the surgeon
options.B: Performing the surgical hand scrub before entering the room
options.C: Closing the surgical skin incision independently
options.D: Monitoring the team and correcting breaks in sterile technique

explanation: Working outside the sterile field allows the circulating nurse to observe the entire room and catch contamination breaks immediately. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h8)

question: Where should used surgical scalpel blades be disposed of immediately after use?

options.A: Cardboard instrument boxes
options.B: Black waste bags
options.C: General washing basins
options.D: Puncture-proof sharps containers

explanation: Sharps must go into puncture-resistant containers to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to staff. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h9)

question: Why are surgical instruments soaked in enzymatic solutions after a procedure?

options.A: To polish the instrument surface to a shine
options.B: To loosen and dissolve dried blood and organic debris
options.C: To cool down hot metal after autoclaving
options.D: To sharpen the metal edges automatically

explanation: Enzymatic cleaners break down proteins and fats, making subsequent washing and sterilization much more effective. [learn more](GST114_U2_T13#GST114_U2_T13_h9)

question: What primary goal does proper medical waste management achieve?

options.A: Speeds up laboratory diagnosis times
options.B: Breaks the chain of infection
options.C: Decreases pharmaceutical drug expenses
options.D: Reduces hospital utility costs

explanation: Proper waste management stops pathogens from spreading to staff, patients, and the environment. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h1)

question: The main danger of failing to sort waste at the bedside is that...

options.A: Nursing documentation takes twice as long
options.B: Laboratory equipment rusts much faster
options.C: Safe waste becomes contaminated hazardous waste
options.D: Hospital electricity bills increase significantly

explanation: Mixing hazardous material with ordinary refuse makes the entire batch dangerously infectious. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which color container is strictly designated for used needles and blades?

options.A: Standard black bin
options.B: Plain brown container
options.C: Transparent plastic bag
options.D: Yellow safety box

explanation: Puncture-proof yellow safety boxes protect workers from accidental needle stick injuries. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h2)

question: Why must waste segregation happen directly at the point of generation?

options.A: To make sure cleaners finish their shifts early
options.B: To reduce the physical weight of the bin bags
options.C: To prevent workers from sorting dangerous items later
options.D: To comply with hospital interior design rules

explanation: Immediate sorting protects downstream handlers from accidentally touching hidden sharps or contaminated materials. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h2)

question: What goes directly inside the secondary packaging when transporting a lab specimen?

options.A: The primary leak-proof receptacle
options.B: The patient clinical case notes
options.C: The external cardboard shipping box
options.D: The hospital administrative stamp

explanation: The primary receptacle holds the actual specimen and goes straight into the secondary container. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is the specific purpose of the absorbent material inside the secondary packaging?

options.A: To neutralize any chemical fumes escaping the specimen tube
options.B: To keep the specimen cool during hot tropical weather
options.C: To soak up the entire liquid volume if the vial breaks
options.D: To prevent the glass tube from rattling against the sides

explanation: Absorbent padding contains fluid spills instantly, stopping leakage outside the secondary container. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h3)

question: Which method serves as the gold standard for sterilizing reusable laboratory tools?

options.A: Autoclaving with pressurized steam
options.B: Submerging in weak vinegar solution
options.C: Exposing to normal room sunlight
options.D: Washing with warm soapy water

explanation: Pressurized steam inside an autoclave destroys all resilient spores and pathogens effectively. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h4)

question: Why is incineration heavily relied upon for anatomical pathology specimens?

options.A: It destroys organic matter completely and leaves nothing recognizable
options.B: It turns the hospital waste into safe fertilizer
options.C: It allows the hospital to recycle metal components easily
options.D: It requires very low energy compared to standard washing

explanation: High-temperature combustion ensures complete destruction of human tissue and heavily infected dressings. [learn more](GST114_U2_T14#GST114_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take after sustaining a needle stick injury?

options.A: Apply a tight tourniquet above the puncture wound
options.B: Wash the site immediately with soap and water
options.C: Write an incident report for the hospital director
options.D: Finish the remaining medication round duties

question: When cleaning a liquid biohazard spill on the floor, why should disinfectant be applied from the edges inward?

question: What defines microbial surveillance in a healthcare setting?

question: Why is establishing a baseline level of pathogens important for a healthcare system?

question: What is the main purpose of using standardized case definitions in data collection?

options.B: They directly observe initial symptoms and track patient changes daily

question: What is the very first step taken when an outbreak is suspected?

question: Analyzing outbreak data by time, place, and person helps public health workers achieve what goal?

options.A: Determine the salary grades for investigative staff

question: Which factor commonly delays outbreak responses in resource-limited health systems?

options.A: Reliance on slow paper-based record systems

options.C: An excess of highly trained epidemiological staff

question: What is a major consequence of lacking reliable laboratory infrastructure during surveillance?

question: What is the primary characteristic of individuals placed in quarantine?

question: Why is the duration of quarantine based on the pathogen's incubation period?

question: A patient with a confirmed Lassa fever diagnosis requires which measure?

question: A key difference between isolation and quarantine is that isolation applies to people who are...

options.C: waiting for test results

question: Which type of quarantine involves restricting movement across an entire neighborhood or town?

question: A returning traveler with no symptoms but potential exposure is advised to stay in their house. What type of quarantine is this?

question: Why is routine temperature measurement essential during the monitoring of quarantined individuals?

question: A quarantined person reports feeling increasingly anxious and trapped in their room. What should the nurse do?

question: What is considered the single most effective intervention in infection prevention and control?

question: Why must personal protective equipment be doffed following specific institutional guidelines?

options.B: To comply with fashion standards in modern hospitals
options.C: To ensure the garments can be washed and reused immediately

question: How does clear patient education reduce anxiety among quarantined individuals?

question: A family in home quarantine expresses fear of community stigma and ostracization. What is the appropriate nursing action?

question: What is the primary purpose of isolation in healthcare settings?

options.B: To reduce hospital running costs

question: A patient with suspected Lassa fever is placed in a single room away from others. This action demonstrates what concept?

question: Isolation precautions primarily interrupt which link in the chain of infection?

question: Breaking the chain of infection using physical barriers protects which group most directly?

options.A: Pathogen reservoirs
options.B: Susceptible hosts
options.C: Infectious agents
options.D: Environmental sources

question: Standard precautions must be used with which category of patients?

question: A nurse wears gloves before touching a patient's intact skin during a routine bath. Why is this practice incorrect under standard precautions?

question: What type of room is required for a patient placed on airborne precautions?

question: What is the first item of PPE that should be removed during doffing?

question: Why should dedicated medical equipment remain inside an isolation room?

question: Which psychological response is commonly observed in patients undergoing prolonged isolation?

options.B: Depression and loneliness
options.C: Memory loss and confusion

question: Reporting a suspected outbreak of a communicable disease is primarily the responsibility of whom?

options.A: The pharmacy technician
options.B: The nurse
options.C: The hospital accountant
options.D: The patient's family

question: What is the primary public health goal of contact tracing?

question: Which link in the chain of infection does contact tracing directly interrupt?

question: What action comes immediately after interviewing a confirmed index case?

question: Why is daily monitoring of contacts maintained throughout the incubation period?

question: A person who sat across a large hall from an infected individual for two minutes is classified as what type of contact?

question: Why does public health practice differentiate between close and casual contacts?

options.C: To reduce the paperwork required for low-risk individuals

options.D: Demanding a rapid, yes-or-no questionnaire response

question: How does patient fear of stigmatization negatively impact the contact tracing process?

question: What is the key difference between quarantine and isolation?

question: A patient with a confirmed laboratory diagnosis of Lassa fever is placed in a separate room away from healthy individuals. What public health measure is this?

question: When notifying an exposed contact, what vital piece of patient information must the nurse protect?

question: Why is maintaining strict confidentiality crucial for the success of contact tracing programs?

options.C: It guarantees financial compensation for quarantined workers

question: Which group is most effective for building local trust during community health outbreaks in Nigeria?

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical logistical challenge faced by contact tracers in many Nigerian settings?

question: What direction do case-control studies look when investigating health outcomes?

options.B: Backward from outcome to exposure

question: Why are case-control studies classified as observational research?

options.B: Laboratory equipment records data automatically
options.C: The study takes place strictly in a classroom
options.D: Participants observe their own symptoms daily

question: What is a major advantage of using case-control designs?

options.A: They prove definitive causation instantly
options.B: They are useful for studying rare diseases
options.C: They eliminate all forms of human bias
options.D: They require no statistical calculations

explanation: Starting with people who already have the condition makes it efficient to study rare health problems that would require huge cohort sizes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: A study design starts with sick patients and healthy neighbors, checking their past diets. What design is this?

options.A: Descriptive case report
options.B: Randomized controlled trial
options.C: Case-control study
options.D: Cross-sectional survey

explanation: Comparing individuals with a condition to those without it while looking at past habits defines a case-control study. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h2)

question: What primary requirement must control participants meet in a case-control study?

options.B: They must be at risk of the disease
options.C: They must have recovered from the illness

question: Why is strict diagnostic criteria for cases necessary in research?

options.B: It prevents participants from dropping out early
options.C: It guarantees that funding will be renewed
options.D: It allows researchers to skip statistical analysis

question: What is recall bias in a retrospective study?

options.B: Differential memory of past exposures by cases
options.C: Patients refusing to answer any survey questions
options.D: The computer deleting historical patient records

question: How can researchers reduce information bias during exposure data collection?

question: What statistical measure is primarily calculated in case-control studies?

explanation: Because case-control studies start with disease status, they calculate the odds ratio rather than direct risk or incidence. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: An odds ratio of 3.5 is calculated for a waterborne infection. What does this mean?

options.A: Exposed persons have higher odds of infection
options.B: Only 3.5 percent of people developed symptoms
options.C: The study had a major methodological error
options.D: The water source is completely safe to drink

explanation: An odds ratio greater than 1 indicates that the exposure is associated with increased odds of developing the condition. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h5)

question: What is a confounding variable in epidemiological research?

options.A: A missing questionnaire from a dropped participant
options.B: The primary disease outcome being measured
options.C: An unmeasured factor skewing the exposure-disease link
options.D: A deliberate intervention performed by the nurse

explanation: Confounders are third variables that relate to both the exposure and the outcome, creating a false impression of cause and effect. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: How does matching help control confounding during the design phase?

options.A: It eliminates all forms of recall bias automatically
options.B: It doubles the total sample size required for testing
options.C: It forces participants to take their prescribed medication
options.D: It ensures cases and controls share similar confounding traits

explanation: Matching pairs cases and controls by key characteristics like age or sex so those factors cannot bias the final comparison. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h6)

question: Which of the following is a major limitation of case-control studies?

options.A: They require huge populations of healthy people
options.B: Inability to calculate absolute disease incidence
options.C: They take many decades to complete fully
options.D: They are too expensive for standard clinical use

explanation: Because researchers select the proportion of cases and controls beforehand, true disease rates in the general population cannot be measured directly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h7)

question: Why are case-control studies poor choices for investigating rare exposures?

options.A: Ethics boards prohibit studying rare substances
options.B: Most sampled patients will not have had the exposure
options.C: Laboratory tests cannot detect rare chemicals accurately
options.D: Statistical software cannot process rare data points

explanation: If an exposure is very rare, you will rarely find it among either cases or controls, making statistical analysis unfeasible. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h7)

question: When are case-control studies most urgently deployed in clinical practice?

options.A: When planning a hospital building renovation
options.B: During routine annual staff performance reviews
options.C: When updating nursing school curricula
options.D: During sudden community disease outbreaks

explanation: Their speed and efficiency make case-control designs the go-to tool for tracing sources during acute public health outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h8)

question: A nurse epidemiologist investigates a sudden cholera spike by interviewing patients and healthy neighbors about water sources. What is the goal?

options.A: To calculate the exact birth rate of the region
options.B: To prove that cholera is transmitted only by air
options.C: To test a new vaccine on the affected community
options.D: To identify the contaminated exposure source quickly

explanation: Comparing what the sick and healthy ingested helps isolate the vehicle of transmission so public health interventions can stop the spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T19#GST114_U2_T19_h8)

question: How many links make up the complete chain of infection?

options.A: Six links
options.B: Eight links
options.C: Ten links
options.D: Four links

explanation: The chain of infection consists of six distinct links that must all be present for an infection to spread. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What happens when you successfully interrupt any single link in the chain of infection?

options.A: The infection changes into a non-communicable disease
options.B: The pathogen becomes stronger and multiplies faster
options.C: The spread of the infection stops completely
options.D: The patient develops lifelong immunity immediately

explanation: Because the chain requires every link to remain unbroken, removing or blocking even one link halts the transmission cycle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h1)

question: What term describes the natural habitat where a pathogen lives and grows?

options.A: A portal of exit
options.B: A reservoir
options.C: A vector carrier
options.D: A susceptible host

explanation: A reservoir provides the necessary conditions for a microorganism to survive and multiply before infecting a new host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is considered a non-living reservoir for hospital-acquired pathogens?

options.A: An asymptomatic patient
options.B: A nurse with an infected cut
options.C: Contaminated sink drainage pipes
options.D: A stray dog in the compound

explanation: Non-living reservoirs include inanimate environmental objects and surfaces like water sources, soil, and damp hospital fixtures. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is a portal of exit in the spread of infection?

options.A: The medical device used to sterilize surgical instruments
options.B: The route a pathogen uses to leave the reservoir
options.C: The method nurses use to discharge a healthy patient
options.D: The medication administered to kill a causative agent

explanation: The portal of exit is the specific pathway through which a pathogen escapes its original host or reservoir. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: A patient inhales airborne tuberculosis droplets into their lungs. What is the respiratory tract acting as in this scenario?

options.A: A causative agent
options.B: A vehicle of transmission
options.C: A portal of entry
options.D: A natural reservoir

explanation: The respiratory tract serves as the physical doorway for the pathogen to enter the body of the new host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h3)

question: Mosquitoes spreading the malaria parasite to a human act as which type of transmission?

options.A: Direct contact transmission
options.B: Vector-borne transmission
options.C: Airborne transmission
options.D: Droplet transmission

explanation: Vectors are living creatures, primarily insects and animals, that transfer infectious agents from one host to another. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: What distinguishes airborne transmission from droplet transmission?

options.A: Droplet transmission only occurs through contaminated drinking water
options.B: Airborne pathogens only spread through direct physical touching
options.C: Droplet particles remain suspended in the air for many hours
options.D: Airborne particles are smaller and remain suspended in the air longer

explanation: Airborne transmission involves tiny droplet nuclei or dust that travel long distances on air currents, unlike heavier droplets that fall quickly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h4)

question: What defines a susceptible host in the chain of infection?

options.A: An inanimate object that harbors microbial spores
options.B: A healthcare worker who washes their hands regularly
options.C: An individual who lacks resistance to a specific pathogen
options.D: A person who has complete immunity against all bacteria

explanation: A susceptible host is someone whose immune system or physical barriers cannot successfully fight off an incoming microorganism. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)

question: Why are surgical patients often considered highly susceptible hosts?

options.A: They produce too many white blood cells during operations
options.B: Their hospital diets contain excessive amounts of protective vitamins
options.C: Their natural skin and tissue barriers have been broken
options.D: They never come into contact with infectious microorganisms

explanation: Invasive surgical procedures breach the primary protective barriers of the body, making it much easier for pathogens to establish an infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which nursing action is most effective for interrupting the mode of transmission?

options.A: Writing accurate fluid balance chart reports
options.B: Checking the patient's temperature every morning
options.C: Performing thorough hand hygiene between patients
options.D: Administering prescribed multivitamin tablets

explanation: Hand hygiene is widely recognized as the single most effective way to prevent the transfer of pathogens from person to person. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h6)

question: How does proper sterilization of surgical instruments break the chain of infection?

options.A: It turns the operating theatre into an active human reservoir
options.B: It destroys the causative agent before it reaches a patient
options.C: It removes the susceptible host from the surgical ward
options.D: It closes off the patient's portal of entry permanently

explanation: Sterilization completely eliminates all forms of microbial life, effectively destroying the causative agent at its potential source. [learn more](GST114_U2_T2#GST114_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of infectious disease surveillance in public health practice?

options.A: Conducting laboratory research on rare genetic disorders
options.B: Treating individual patients with chronic illnesses
options.C: Managing hospital financial budgets and staffing levels
options.D: Collecting data for health planning and epidemic control

explanation: Surveillance systematically gathers health data to plan interventions and control disease outbreaks across populations. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: Why must primary health centres link their data to national health agencies like the NCDC?

options.A: To reduce the total number of required nursing documentation tasks
options.B: To simplify the payroll processing for rural healthcare workers
options.C: To secure direct international funding for local clinic repairs
options.D: To enable early detection and response to potential epidemics

explanation: Connecting local facilities to a national grid ensures rapid identification and containment of spreading pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h1)

question: What primary Nigerian law empowers authorities to enforce disease quarantine and notification?

options.A: The Consumer Protection Council Law
options.B: The Quarantine Act
options.C: The Nursing and Midwifery Decree
options.D: The National Health Insurance Act

explanation: The Quarantine Act provides the legal backing for public health officers to manage outbreaks and enforce reporting. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Why is disease notification made a mandatory legal duty for healthcare workers?

options.A: To evaluate individual nurse productivity and clinical performance
options.B: To maintain complex bureaucratic paperwork in federal archives
options.C: To ensure rapid containment before localized clusters become widespread
options.D: To increase government revenue through statutory reporting fines
