explanation: Mandatory reporting forces immediate administrative action, stopping community transmission chains early. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h2)

question: Which timeframe is required for reporting a Category 1 emergency notifiable disease?

options.A: During the annual health audit
options.B: At the end of every month
options.C: Within 7 days
options.D: Within 24 hours

explanation: Category 1 conditions carry high mortality risks and demand immediate notification within a day. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: A patient presents with sudden severe watery diarrhoea and dehydration during a suspected cholera outbreak. This condition belongs to which category?

options.A: Category 2
options.B: Category 1
options.C: Category 4
options.D: Category 3

explanation: Cholera is a highly transmissible epidemic-prone disease requiring immediate emergency reporting within 24 hours. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h3)

question: Why are nurses considered the frontline personnel in disease surveillance?

options.A: They write all international health quarantine laws and guidelines
options.B: They hold sole legal responsibility for national laboratory testing
options.C: They are usually the first professional point of contact for patients
options.D: They manage the federal health ministry's disease budget allocations

explanation: As initial evaluators of sick individuals, nurses spot early warning signs of infectious outbreaks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: What immediate clinical action should a nurse take upon identifying a suspected case of a severe notifiable disease?

options.A: Discharge the patient immediately with oral home remedies
options.B: Wait for laboratory confirmation before taking any safety steps
options.C: Initiate isolation procedures and document clinical history
options.D: Transfer the patient to an open general waiting ward

explanation: Prompt isolation prevents further transmission within the facility while accurate documentation aids reporting. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h4)

question: Who is the primary local officer notified immediately after a suspected case is detected in a clinic?

options.A: The international health organization desk director
options.B: The federal minister of finance and economic planning
options.C: The facility Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer
options.D: The local pharmaceutical manufacturing supervisor

explanation: The DSNO is the designated officer responsible for coordinating local reporting and institutional response. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using standardized IDSR forms during disease reporting?

options.A: To ensure consistent data collection across all levels of health care
options.B: To evaluate nursing school admission qualifications and test scores
options.C: To calculate exact hospital utility bills and electricity usage
options.D: To provide patients with comprehensive personal medical insurance policies

explanation: Standardized forms prevent miscommunication and ensure uniform data formatting from local clinics to national databases. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of contact tracing during a disease outbreak?

options.A: Identifying and monitoring individuals exposed to an infectious case
options.B: Auditing hospital financial records and purchasing receipts
options.C: Cleaning and sterilizing commercial market spaces and offices
options.D: Conducting clinical drug trials for newly invented vaccines

explanation: Contact tracing locates exposed persons so they can be monitored and isolated before spreading infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Why must contacts of an infectious patient be monitored throughout the entire incubation period?

options.A: Patients refuse to take medications without daily nursing supervision
options.B: Government regulations mandate exactly fourteen days of hospital stay
options.C: Laboratory tests are completely useless before the incubation window
options.D: Symptoms may appear at any time within that specific window

explanation: Monitoring covers the full incubation duration to catch symptom onset early and prevent hidden transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which precautions apply universally to the care of all patients regardless of their diagnosis?

options.A: Standard precautions
options.B: Quarantine enforcement protocols
options.C: Contact tracing guidelines
options.D: Airborne isolation precautions

explanation: Standard precautions are baseline infection control practices meant for every patient interaction. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: A nurse cares for a patient with a confirmed airborne pathogen in an isolation ward. Which control measure is most critical to implement?

options.A: Using appropriate respiratory protection and proper ventilation
options.B: Administering broad-spectrum oral vitamins to all visitors
options.C: Conducting routine physical exercise therapy in open hallways
options.D: Performing daily financial audits of ward equipment supplies

explanation: Airborne pathogens require specialized respiratory gear and ventilation control to prevent aerosol inhalation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h7)

question: What is a common community-level challenge that hinders effective disease surveillance and reporting?

options.A: Immediate compliance with all government health directives
options.B: Oversupply of reporting forms in primary health centers
options.C: Excessive availability of advanced diagnostic laboratory equipment
options.D: Fear of quarantine and cultural stigma driving cases underground

explanation: Stigma and fear cause communities to hide infections, delaying detection and public health response. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)

question: Why is digitizing reporting systems considered an effective mitigation strategy for surveillance challenges?

options.A: It removes the need for standard infection prevention supplies
options.B: It eliminates the need for any healthcare workers in remote clinics
options.C: It enables real-time data transmission from rural areas to national centers
options.D: It completely stops infectious pathogens from mutating in the environment

explanation: Digital tools bypass postal and physical delivery delays, allowing authorities to view outbreaks instantly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T20#GST114_U2_T20_h8)

question: Who should standard precautions apply to in the hospital?

options.A: Individuals showing visible symptoms of disease
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients with confirmed viral infections
options.D: All patients regardless of their diagnosis

explanation: Standard precautions are used for every patient care encounter to prevent exposure, regardless of their diagnosis. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h1)

question: Which body fluid is excluded from standard precautions?

options.A: Cerebrospinal fluid from a lumbar puncture
options.B: Vomitus containing small blood streaks
options.C: Saliva during dental procedures
options.D: Sweat from a febrile patient

explanation: Intact skin and sweat do not transmit bloodborne pathogens, so they are excluded unless they contain visible blood. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h1)

question: How long should you rub your hands together when using an alcohol-based hand sanitizer?

options.A: 20 to 30 seconds
options.B: 3 to 5 minutes
options.C: 1 to 2 minutes
options.D: 5 to 10 seconds

explanation: Applying friction for 20 to 30 seconds ensures that all surfaces of the hands are properly sanitized. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h2)

question: A patient has Clostridium difficile colitis. What is the correct hand hygiene method?

options.A: Washing hands thoroughly with soap and water
options.B: Rinsing hands briefly under running tap water
options.C: Applying a rapid-drying alcohol hand sanitizer
options.D: Wiping hands with a dry sterile gauze pad

explanation: Alcohol hand rubs cannot kill bacterial spores, so you must physically wash them away with soap and water. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h2)

question: Which piece of protective gear requires you to perform a user seal check after putting it on?

options.A: N95 particulate respirator
options.B: Standard surgical face mask
options.C: Non-sterile examination gloves
options.D: Disposable plastic apron

explanation: A seal check makes sure the N95 fits tightly against your face to block airborne particles. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h3)

question: You are about to flush out a large, infected wound. What PPE should you wear?

options.A: Sterile gloves and an isolation gown only
options.B: Mask, eye protection, gown, and gloves
options.C: Face shield and sterile surgical cap only
options.D: N95 respirator and clean examination gloves

explanation: Wound irrigation causes fluid splashes, so you need full facial and body protection to stay safe. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h3)

question: What is the key safety rule when handling used injection needles?

options.A: Store used needles in kidney dishes at the bedside
options.B: Break the needle off the syringe before disposal
options.C: Always recap needles firmly before walking to the bin
options.D: Never recap needles using a two-handed technique

explanation: Using both hands to recap a needle is a major cause of accidental needle-prick injuries. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h4)

question: A sharps container in the treatment room is three-quarters full. What should you do?

options.A: Close and seal the container for safe disposal
options.B: Transfer half the contents into a smaller empty box
options.C: Leave it open until the end of the current shift
options.D: Press the contents down to create more usable space

explanation: Sharps containers should never be overfilled or compressed; seal and replace them when they reach the fill line. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h4)

question: If you do not have a tissue, where should you cough or sneeze?

options.A: Straight down toward the floor
options.B: Directly into both open palms
options.C: Into the inner bend of the elbow
options.D: Outward into the open air

explanation: Coughing into your elbow stops germs from getting onto your hands, where they can spread to surfaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h5)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic coughing constantly and producing thick sputum. What should you do first?

options.A: Draw blood samples for a complete blood count immediately
options.B: Admit the patient directly to the intensive care unit for isolation
options.C: Administer a broad-spectrum oral antibiotic without a doctor's order
options.D: Provide a surgical mask and guide the patient to a separate seating area

explanation: Giving the patient a mask and moving them away from others helps stop the spread of airborne droplets in waiting areas. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h5)

question: Which surface in a patient's room needs to be cleaned and disinfected most often?

options.A: Interior walls away from the bed
options.B: Bedside rails and call buttons
options.C: The ceiling tiles above the bed
options.D: The underside of the patient mattress

explanation: High-touch surfaces are handled constantly by patients and staff, making them easy spreaders of germs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h6)

question: Why is it important to follow the correct contact time when using a hospital disinfectant?

options.A: It ensures the solution dries without leaving water marks
options.B: It guarantees the chemical kills the targeted microorganisms
options.C: It prevents the cleaning cloth from sticking to the surface
options.D: It stops the solution from producing toxic chemical fumes

explanation: Disinfectants need to stay wet on a surface for a specific amount of time to actually destroy germs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h6)

question: Which type of waste goes into a yellow bin with a biohazard symbol?

options.A: Soiled dressings and blood-soaked gauze
options.B: Leftover food scraps from patient trays
options.C: Office paper and administrative notes
options.D: Empty cardboard boxes from supplies

explanation: Yellow biohazard bins are meant for items that have body fluids on them. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h7)

question: Why do hospitals sort waste right at the spot where it is generated?

options.A: Reducing the physical weight of bins carried by housekeeping
options.B: Lowering the cost of purchasing heavy-duty plastic liners
options.C: Preventing injury and contamination during handling and disposal
options.D: Ensuring all hospital refuse can be recycled into new plastics

explanation: Sorting waste immediately keeps hazardous materials managed safely and protects waste handlers. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h7)

question: What is the first thing a nurse should do after accidentally getting poked by a used needle?

options.A: Wash the puncture site immediately with soap and water
options.B: Apply a tight tourniquet above the site of injury
options.C: Report to the hospital administration at the end of the shift
options.D: Squeeze the wound hard to force out trapped blood

explanation: Washing the site right away helps lower the amount of germs entering the body before further medical checks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h8)

question: Why must a nurse report an accidental needle-prick injury right away?

options.A: To prove negligence on the part of the hospital management
options.B: To avoid disciplinary action from the nursing council
options.C: To secure financial compensation for emotional distress
options.D: To allow timely administration of post-exposure prophylaxis

explanation: Preventive medicines work best when started within hours of an exposure incident. [learn more](GST114_U2_T21#GST114_U2_T21_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of a hospital infection control unit?

options.A: To manage patient billing records
options.B: To break the chain of infection
options.C: To reduce hospital running costs
options.D: To supervise pharmacy drug dispensing

explanation: Infection control focuses on interrupting transmission pathways to protect everyone in the facility. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h1)

question: Why are healthcare-associated infections considered a major concern in clinical practice?

options.A: They reduce the need for routine hospital cleaning
options.B: They decrease the total number of hospital admissions
options.C: They only affect nurses and doctors on duty
options.D: They prolong patient stays and increase costs

explanation: Infections acquired in the hospital worsen patient outcomes and strain financial and medical resources. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h1)

question: Who typically serves as the core professional responsible for daily ward surveillance?

options.A: The Infection Control Nurse
options.B: The Director of Maintenance
options.C: The Hospital Chief Accountant
options.D: The Lead Pharmacist

explanation: Infection control nurses drive daily surveillance, staff training, and compliance auditing on the wards. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h2)

question: A hospital needs to track rising antibiotic resistance patterns on the wards. Which team member is primarily responsible for this lab analysis?

options.A: The Biomedical Engineer
options.B: The Human Resources Manager
options.C: The Microbiologist
options.D: The Estate Surveyor

explanation: Microbiologists examine laboratory specimens to identify specific pathogens and their resistance profiles. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h2)

question: What does active surveillance by the infection control team involve?

options.A: Waiting for patients to report symptoms at home
options.B: Inspecting the hospital kitchen food supplies daily
options.C: Conducting annual financial audits for the facility
options.D: Reviewing patient charts and lab reports on wards

explanation: Active surveillance requires staff to purposefully search for infection indicators rather than relying on passive reporting. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h3)

question: Why is establishing baseline infection rates important for a healthcare facility?

options.A: It helps signal immediate warnings when infection numbers spike
options.B: It guarantees zero hospital-acquired infections occur
options.C: It eliminates the need for any future hand hygiene audits
options.D: It determines the monthly salaries of clinical staff members

explanation: Knowing the normal baseline allows the unit to quickly identify unusual outbreaks or rising infection trends. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of infection control policies in a hospital?

options.A: To provide standardized rules guiding safe clinical practice
options.B: To determine the pricing structure of laboratory tests
options.C: To outline the promotion criteria for nursing personnel
options.D: To restrict patient visitation hours across all wards

explanation: Policies establish clear, uniform expectations for how staff should perform clinical procedures safely. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h4)

question: Why must hospital infection control policies undergo regular review?

options.A: To reduce the total number of employed nurses
options.B: To change the names of hospital wards annually
options.C: To comply with local tax regulations for businesses
options.D: To ensure guidelines reflect current scientific evidence

explanation: Medical knowledge evolves, requiring policies to update in line with new evidence and health standards. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h4)

question: What do standard precautions primarily serve as in a healthcare setting?

options.A: A foundational barrier between patients and infectious agents
options.B: A maintenance schedule for hospital diagnostic machines
options.C: A scheduling tool for nurses working night shifts
options.D: A financial incentive scheme for senior medical doctors

explanation: Standard precautions treat all body fluids as potentially infectious, creating a barrier of protection for everyone. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h5)

question: How does continuous staff education impact infection control within a hospital?

options.A: It replaces the need for cleaning supplies on the wards
options.B: It stops patients from being admitted to the emergency unit
options.C: It bridges the gap between written policy and bedside behavior
options.D: It automatically diagnoses resistant bacterial infections

explanation: Regular training reinforces good habits, ensuring staff actually apply safety guidelines during patient care. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h5)

question: When is a hospital outbreak officially recognized by the infection control unit?

options.A: When the hospital changes its visiting hours schedule
options.B: When infection cases exceed what is normally expected
options.C: When annual financial reports are published
options.D: When a new batch of medical supplies arrives

explanation: An outbreak is defined by an unusual increase in infection frequency above the baseline rate. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h6)

question: A ward reports an unexpected cluster of multidrug-resistant wound infections. What is the immediate priority action for the unit?

options.A: Verify the diagnosis and trace the source of infection
options.B: Order new uniforms for all nursing staff on duty
options.C: Discharge all admitted patients immediately without review
options.D: Close the entire hospital down for major renovations

explanation: Stopping an outbreak requires investigating the source to implement targeted control measures effectively. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h6)

question: Why is the proper segregation of medical waste at the point of generation important?

options.A: It ensures that hospital laundry is washed at high temperatures
options.B: It protects sanitary workers and the community from injury
options.C: It speeds up the admission process for new patients
options.D: It reduces the cost of purchasing pharmaceutical drugs

explanation: Segregating waste correctly prevents sharps injuries and infectious exposure for handlers and the public. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h7)

question: How do contaminated environmental surfaces contribute to hospital-acquired infections?

options.A: They cause immediate equipment failure in the radiology unit
options.B: They prevent nursing staff from documenting patient vitals
options.C: They alter the chemical composition of intravenous fluids
options.D: Pathogens transfer easily to patients via hands or touch

explanation: Surfaces act as reservoirs where germs linger until touched by healthcare workers or patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h7)

question: Why does the infection control unit report notifiable diseases to health authorities?

options.A: To help monitor community-wide epidemic threats
options.B: To determine the retail pricing of surgical instruments
options.C: To evaluate the clinical performance of individual nurses
options.D: To request funding for new hospital building projects

explanation: Reporting notifiable diseases allows public health bodies to track and respond to broader outbreaks outside the hospital. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h8)

question: How does partnership with the infection control unit empower bedside nurses?

options.A: It removes all documentation duties from their daily shifts
options.B: It equips them to act as frontline defenders for patient safety
options.C: It allows them to diagnose complex infectious diseases alone
options.D: It exempts them from administering prescribed medications

explanation: Working closely with infection control gives nurses the knowledge and backing to maintain strict safety standards. [learn more](GST114_U2_T22#GST114_U2_T22_h8)

question: What is the term for structural disruptions in host tissues caused by pathogens?

options.A: Cellular hyperplasia
options.B: Genetic mutations
options.C: Benign neoplasia
options.D: Infectious lesions

explanation: Infectious lesions describe the visible or microscopic damage inflicted on body tissues by invading microorganisms. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Pathogenesis describes which aspect of a disease process?

options.A: The laboratory staining technique for bacteria
options.B: The surgical removal of damaged tissue
options.C: The pharmacological classification of antibiotics
options.D: The biological mechanism leading to disease

explanation: Pathogenesis maps out the specific steps and biological events through which a pathogen establishes infection and causes tissue damage. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which bacterial components are found in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria and trigger severe inflammation?

options.A: Capsular polysaccharides
options.B: Endotoxins
options.C: Flagellar proteins
options.D: Exotoxins

explanation: Endotoxins are lipid-sugar complexes embedded in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria that provoke potent inflammatory reactions when released. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: Host immune-mediated tissue injury occurs primarily because of which factor?

options.A: Aggressive immune responses destroying healthy cells
options.B: Complete absence of white blood cells at the site
options.C: Direct replication of viruses inside blood vessels
options.D: Nutritional depletion caused by fungal overgrowth

explanation: Sometimes the body's own defense mechanisms cause collateral damage to normal tissues during the fight to eliminate a pathogen. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: Which white blood cell type arrives first at the site of an acute infection?

options.A: Eosinophils
options.B: Basophils
options.C: Lymphocytes
options.D: Neutrophils

explanation: Neutrophils are the primary and most abundant responders deployed to acute infection sites to phagocytose invading microbes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: Pus found within an acute abscess is primarily composed of which elements?

options.A: Excess plasma proteins and fibrous scar
options.B: Dead neutrophils and liquefied tissue
options.C: Dormant spores and epithelial cells
options.D: Accumulated red blood cells and platelets

explanation: Purulent exudate or pus consists largely of spent neutrophils, cellular debris, and fluid accumulated during acute inflammatory responses. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary cellular component found within a chronic granulomatous lesion?

options.A: Mature erythrocytes
options.B: Epithelioid macrophages
options.C: Squamous epithelial cells
options.D: Platelet aggregates

explanation: Granulomas are nodular collections of modified, flattened macrophages known as epithelioid cells that wall off difficult-to-clear agents. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: Why does the body form granulomas around certain persistent pathogens?

options.A: To prevent the migration of red blood cells
options.B: To contain organisms that resist normal clearance
options.C: To supply extra nutrients to healthy tissues
options.D: To speed up the healing of superficial wounds

explanation: Granuloma formation acts as an isolating mechanism when the immune system cannot completely eliminate chronic pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a common tissue effect specifically associated with viral replication inside host cells?

options.A: Cytopathic effects
options.B: Caseous liquefaction
options.C: Neutrophil aggregation
options.D: Granuloma calcification

explanation: Viruses disrupt cellular structures and functions during replication, producing recognizable structural changes known as cytopathic effects. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which inflammatory cell type typically predominates in viral infections compared to acute pyogenic bacterial infections?

options.A: Lymphocytes
options.B: Neutrophils
options.C: Basophils
options.D: Eosinophils

explanation: Viral pathogens prompt cell-mediated immune responses, leading to a predominance of lymphocytes rather than the neutrophils seen in acute bacterial pus formation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which white blood cell type is typically elevated during parasitic infestations?

options.A: Eosinophils
options.B: Thrombocytes
options.C: Neutrophils
options.D: Erythrocytes

explanation: Eosinophils specialize in combating multicellular parasites and are characteristically elevated in parasitic infections and associated tissue lesions. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)

question: Fungal tissue lesions most closely resemble the chronic patterns seen in which bacterial infection?

options.A: Tuberculosis
options.B: Staphylococcal cellulitis
options.C: Streptococcal pharyngitis
options.D: Gonococcal urethritis

explanation: Deep fungal infections frequently provoke granulomatous inflammation with necrosis that mimics the histological appearance of tuberculosis. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)

question: What is a key nursing action when monitoring a patient with an infectious skin lesion?

options.A: Ordering diagnostic blood cultures independently
options.B: Inspecting the wound site for spreading inflammation
options.C: Performing surgical debridement of necrotic tissue
options.D: Administering intravenous nutritional supplements daily

explanation: Regular physical inspection helps nurses detect early signs of worsening local infection or spreading cellulitis. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why must nurses consider a patient's immune status when evaluating infectious lesions?

options.A: Granuloma formation only occurs in healthy individuals
options.B: Immunocompromised patients may show muted inflammatory signs
options.C: Antibiotics work exclusively in patients with high neutrophil counts
options.D: Normal immune systems prevent all forms of viral replication

explanation: Patients with weakened immune responses may not exhibit the classic redness, heat, or pus formation, masking the true severity of an infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary event that starts an infectious process in the body?

options.A: Complete failure of the immune system
options.B: Rapid increase in red blood cell production
options.C: Invasion and multiplication of a pathogen
options.D: Sudden drop in body temperature

explanation: Infection begins when foreign microorganisms enter a susceptible host and start reproducing, overcoming the body's initial barriers. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h1)

question: The main difference between a localized infection and a systemic infection is that a systemic infection...

options.A: affects only a single tissue layer
options.B: only occurs in hospitalized patients
options.C: never causes changes in vital signs
options.D: spreads throughout the entire body

explanation: While localized infections stay confined to one area, systemic infections disseminate via the bloodstream to affect multiple organ systems. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h1)

question: During which stage of infection do vague, nonspecific symptoms like mild fatigue first appear?

options.A: Prodromal stage
options.B: Illness stage
options.C: Convalescent stage
options.D: Incubation period

explanation: The prodromal stage is characterized by early, generalized complaints before distinct disease-specific symptoms manifest. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h2)

question: Why is the incubation period challenging for controlling the spread of communicable diseases?

options.A: Patients require immediate intensive care hospitalization before symptoms start.
options.B: Pathogens are completely inactive and cannot cause any harm during this phase.
options.C: The infected person feels healthy and can transmit the pathogen unknowingly.
options.D: Diagnostic tests always fail to detect antibodies during these early days.

explanation: Because individuals show no outward signs of illness during incubation, they often continue normal social routines while shedding pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h2)

question: What part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat during a fever?

options.A: Cerebellum
options.B: Medulla oblongata
options.C: Thalamus
options.D: Hypothalamus

explanation: Chemical mediators called pyrogens signal the hypothalamus to elevate the core body temperature set point. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why does a patient experience shaking chills when their body temperature is starting to rise?

options.A: Excessive sweating leads to rapid evaporative cooling of the skin surface.
options.B: Peripheral blood vessels dilate to release trapped heat from internal organs.
options.C: Rapid muscle contractions generate internal heat to match the new higher set point.
options.D: The nervous system is suffering from permanent cellular damage due to toxins.

explanation: Chills are involuntary muscle shivers that produce metabolic heat to help the core temperature reach the elevated hypothalamic target. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h3)

question: The classic cardinal sign of inflammation described as localized swelling is called...

options.A: erythema
options.B: necrosis
options.C: edema
options.D: cyanosis

explanation: Edema results from fluid shifting out of permeable capillaries into the interstitial spaces surrounding the infected tissue. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h4)

question: What causes the localized pain associated with an acute inflammatory response?

options.A: Rapid decrease in local tissue temperature and blood supply
options.B: Direct destruction of sensory neurons by bacterial toxins
options.C: Complete cessation of electrical activity in local muscle fibers
options.D: Pressure from accumulated fluid stimulating local nerve endings

explanation: Swelling stretches surrounding tissues and puts mechanical pressure on nociceptors, generating pain signals. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h4)

question: A laboratory report showing an elevated white blood cell count is documented as...

options.A: leukocytosis
options.B: polycythemia
options.C: thrombocytosis
options.D: leukopenia

explanation: Leukocytosis represents the active proliferation and release of white blood cells to combat invading pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h5)

question: What does a 'left shift' in a differential white blood cell count typically indicate?

options.A: Recovery from illness and depletion of stored immune cells
options.B: An acute, severe bacterial infection requiring rapid bone marrow output
options.C: A chronic viral infection that has lasted for several months
options.D: A normal physiological response to heavy physical exercise

explanation: When mature neutrophils run out, the bone marrow pumps out immature forms, known as bands, signaling a heavy infectious demand. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h5)

question: An elderly patient with a urinary tract infection is most likely to present with which atypical symptom?

options.A: Marked decrease in respiratory rate
options.B: High fever and severe joint stiffness
options.C: Acute confusion and behavioral changes
options.D: Sudden paralysis of the lower limbs

explanation: Older adults frequently exhibit delirium or altered mental status instead of typical fever when dealing with systemic infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common gastrointestinal sign of a systemic infection?

options.A: Nausea and vomiting
options.B: Loss of appetite
options.C: Uncontrolled polyuria
options.D: Watery diarrhea

explanation: Polyuria relates to urinary or endocrine issues rather than being a primary gastrointestinal sign of infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why does an increased heart rate (tachycardia) commonly occur during a systemic infection?

options.A: To slow down blood flow and trap pathogens in peripheral tissues
options.B: To circulate oxygen and immune cells faster to meet metabolic needs
options.C: To prevent the kidneys from producing excess urine
options.D: To compensate for a sudden drop in core body temperature

explanation: Fever and infection increase metabolic rate, forcing the cardiovascular system to pump blood faster to maintain tissue oxygenation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h7)

question: A patient with a severe infection shows a dropping blood pressure and cold, clammy skin. What does this suggest?

options.A: A normal recovery phase as the fever begins to break
options.B: Progression toward septic shock and circulatory collapse
options.C: Successful response to oral antibiotic therapy
options.D: Localized inflammation limited to the skin surface

explanation: Hypotension and poor perfusion during infection indicate that the body can no longer maintain adequate vascular tone, signaling shock. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why is strict adherence to scheduled antibiotic administration critical in treating infections?

options.A: It prevents the patient from experiencing common gastrointestinal side effects.
options.B: It allows the nurse to finish the shift work without medication delays.
options.C: It maintains consistent therapeutic drug levels in the bloodstream to kill pathogens.
options.D: It guarantees that white blood cell production will immediately cease.

explanation: Consistent dosing prevents drops in medication concentration that could allow resistant strains of bacteria to survive and multiply. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h8)

question: Which nursing action is most effective in preventing the nosocomial spread of infectious agents?

options.A: Restricting all family visitors from entering the hospital ward
options.B: Increasing the room temperature to inhibit airborne bacterial growth
options.C: Administering antipyretic medications every four hours around the clock
options.D: Performing proper hand hygiene before and after patient contact

explanation: Hand hygiene remains the single most effective infection control measure to break the chain of transmission in healthcare settings. [learn more](GST114_U2_T4#GST114_U2_T4_h8)

question: What are the three core elements of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Vector, parasite, and reservoir
options.B: Infection, disease, and recovery
options.C: Agent, host, and environment
options.D: Source, transmission, and susceptible person

explanation: The epidemiological triangle consists of the agent, the host, and the environment interacting to produce disease. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h1)

question: How does improving poor housing sanitation primarily impact the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: It permanently alters the genetic makeup of the host.
options.B: It directly destroys the pathogenic agent inside the body.
options.C: It increases the overall susceptibility of the human host.
options.D: It modifies the environment to reduce disease transmission.

explanation: Housing and sanitation fall under environmental factors that influence whether an infectious agent reaches a host. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h1)

question: A contaminated hospital water supply acts as which link in the chain of infection?

options.A: Reservoir
options.B: Infectious agent
options.C: Portal of exit
options.D: Susceptible host

explanation: A reservoir is the natural environment where a pathogen lives, grows, and multiplies, such as water or soil. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h2)

question: Applying hand hygiene before touching a patient primarily blocks which link in the chain?

options.A: Portal of exit
options.B: Mode of transmission
options.C: Infectious agent
options.D: Internal reservoir

explanation: Handwashing prevents healthcare workers from transferring pathogens from one surface or patient to another. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h2)

question: When should standard precautions be applied in clinical practice?

options.A: Only when caring for patients with confirmed viral infections
options.B: During the care of all patients regardless of diagnosis
options.C: Exclusively inside intensive care units and isolation wards
options.D: Whenever a patient displays visible signs of a contagious illness

explanation: Standard precautions are foundational practices applied universally to every patient interaction to prevent bloodborne and contact transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h3)

question: What type of personal protective equipment is required for caring for a patient on airborne precautions?

options.A: An N95 or higher respirator mask
options.B: A standard cloth face covering
options.C: A clean non-sterile surgical mask
options.D: Protective face shield without a mask

explanation: Airborne pathogens require specialized respiratory protection like an N95 respirator to filter out tiny suspended droplet nuclei. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which process achieves the complete destruction of all forms of microbial life including spores?

options.A: Disinfection
options.B: Sterilization
options.C: Sanitization
options.D: Antisepsis

explanation: Sterilization is the only process that destroys all microbial life, including highly resistant bacterial endospores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why is thorough cleaning required before performing chemical disinfection or sterilization?

options.A: Organic matter can shield microorganisms and neutralize chemical agents.
options.B: Water helps soften the metal so it can absorb chemical vapors better.
options.C: Soap acts as a catalyst to speed up the sterilization temperature.
options.D: Cleaning adds a protective chemical layer that prevents future rust.

explanation: Blood, tissue, or dirt left on equipment can block disinfectants from reaching pathogens and deactivate chemical agents. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h4)

question: What type of immunity is developed after receiving a live-attenuated vaccine?

options.A: Passive artificial immunity
options.B: Passive natural immunity
options.C: Active artificial immunity
options.D: Active natural immunity

explanation: Vaccines introduce antigens artificially to stimulate the body's own immune system to create active immunity. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h5)

question: How does high community vaccination coverage protect unvaccinated infants?

options.A: It destroys environmental reservoirs where viruses multiply.
options.B: It alters the genetic susceptibility of the local population.
options.C: It transfers maternal antibodies directly through breast milk.
options.D: It establishes herd immunity by limiting pathogen circulation.

explanation: When the vast majority of a population is immune, outbreaks stall because the pathogen cannot easily find susceptible hosts. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of antimicrobial stewardship programs?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of hospital cleaning supplies
options.B: To optimize antimicrobial use and combat drug resistance
options.C: To completely replace antibiotics with herbal alternatives
options.D: To discover novel synthetic vaccines for viral pathogens

explanation: Stewardship programs ensure proper drug selection, dose, and duration to preserve antimicrobial efficacy. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why is collecting microbiological cultures BEFORE starting antibiotic therapy important?

options.A: Cultures take several days to process in the central laboratory.
options.B: Pre-treatment cultures guarantee that the patient will recover faster.
options.C: Laboratory regulations prohibit testing patients on active medication.
options.D: Antibiotics can alter test results by suppressing pathogen growth.

explanation: Initiating antibiotics first can kill the bacteria before they are isolated in the lab, leading to false-negative cultures. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary difference between isolation and quarantine?

options.A: Isolation is used for bacteria, while quarantine is strictly for viral illnesses.
options.B: Quarantine uses protective gear, while isolation requires negative pressure.
options.C: Isolation separates sick people, while quarantine restricts exposed healthy people.
options.D: Quarantine requires hospitalization, whereas isolation is done at home.

explanation: Isolation applies to those already diagnosed with an infection, while quarantine applies to asymptomatic individuals who had potential exposure. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h7)

question: A healthy traveler arriving from an area with an active fever outbreak is asked to stay home for 14 days. What intervention is this?

options.A: Standard precaution
options.B: Isolation
options.C: Prophylaxis
options.D: Quarantine

explanation: Quarantine monitors exposed, asymptomatic individuals during the incubation period to catch potential disease onset early. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of public health disease surveillance?

options.A: To replace clinical diagnosis with centralized computer tracking
options.B: To monitor health data and detect unusual disease trends
options.C: To punish hospitals that fail to report patient statistics
options.D: To calculate the annual budget for pharmaceutical companies

explanation: Surveillance systems systematically track disease data to identify outbreaks and guide public health responses. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h8)

question: Why is prompt reporting of communicable diseases by frontline nurses vital?

options.A: It prevents patients from developing chronic secondary complications.
options.B: It enables authorities to initiate rapid containment and contact tracing.
options.C: It automatically guarantees funding for local treatment centers.
options.D: It removes the need for standard hand hygiene in the ward.

explanation: Early notification gives public health agencies the time needed to trace exposed individuals and prevent wider community transmission. [learn more](GST114_U2_T5#GST114_U2_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary action of clinical hand washing with soap and water?

options.A: Mechanical removal of dirt and micro-organisms
options.B: Chemical destruction of all bacterial spores
options.C: Complete sterilization of skin layers
options.D: Thermal eradication of resident pathogens

explanation: Soap and water physically lift and wash away transient dirt and microbes from the skin surface through friction and water flow. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why is hand washing considered the most critical barrier in hospitals?

options.A: It permanently destroys all skin microflora instantly
options.B: It stops cross-contamination between patients and staff
options.C: It replaces the need for wearing sterile surgical gloves
options.D: It eliminates airborne pathogens within ward spaces

explanation: Hands act as the primary vehicle for transferring pathogens from one surface or patient to another during routine care. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which type of skin flora is acquired during direct patient care and easily washed off?

options.A: Colonized spores
options.B: Dermal fungi
options.C: Resident flora
options.D: Transient flora

explanation: Transient microbes are picked up from the environment or patients and sit loosely on the skin, making them easy to remove with basic hand washing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the primary characteristic of resident skin flora?

options.A: They live deep in the skin layers and protect against invaders
options.B: They multiply rapidly on the skin surface after touching equipment
options.C: They are highly virulent and cause immediate clinical infections
options.D: They are completely eradicated by a single standard hand wash

explanation: Resident flora inhabit deeper skin strata, are permanent fixtures of the skin microbiome, and help deter harmful pathogens from colonizing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h2)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is directly interrupted by hand washing?

options.A: Mode of transmission
options.B: Portal of exit
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Infectious reservoir

explanation: Hand hygiene stops pathogens from moving between surfaces and patients by eliminating them from the hands acting as the transit vehicle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h3)

question: A nurse forgets to clean hands after touching an infected drain. What role do the hands play in the chain of infection?

options.A: Primary infectious reservoir
options.B: Direct portal of exit
options.C: Vehicle for transmission
options.D: New susceptible host

explanation: Contaminated hands transfer pathogens directly from a source to a new location or patient, serving as the transmission vehicle. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which hand hygiene type is required before assisting in an open surgical theatre procedure?

options.A: Social hand wash
options.B: Hygienic hand rub
options.C: Surgical hand scrub
options.D: Routine water rinse

explanation: A surgical scrub requires extended antimicrobial friction to significantly reduce both transient and resident flora before sterile operations. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h4)

question: When is a social hand wash using plain soap and water most appropriate?

options.A: Immediately before performing an invasive surgical incision
options.B: When rushing between non-touch medication administration rounds
options.C: As a replacement for alcohol rubs on clean ward rounds
options.D: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt or body fluids

explanation: Plain soap and water mechanical action is necessary when organic material or visible dirt is present, as alcohol rubs cannot penetrate heavy soil. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h4)

question: According to the WHO moments, when should a nurse clean hands after adjusting an intravenous infusion line?

options.A: After touching patient surroundings
options.B: Before clean or aseptic procedures
options.C: After body fluid exposure risk
options.D: Before touching a patient

explanation: Managing an IV line is an aseptic task requiring hand hygiene beforehand to prevent introducing pathogens directly into the bloodstream. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why does the WHO framework require hand hygiene after merely touching a patient's bedside table?

options.A: Surroundings become contaminated with patient flora and transmit germs
options.B: It replaces the need to wash hands after physical patient examination
options.C: Bedside tables harbor resident skin flora unique to hospital staff
options.D: Hospital regulations mandate cleaning after touching any wooden surface

explanation: Objects in the immediate patient zone quickly pick up shed skin cells and microbes, acting as vehicles to spread infection if hands are not cleaned. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the recommended duration for performing a standard clinical hand wash with soap and water?

options.A: 40 to 60 seconds
options.B: 10 to 15 seconds
options.C: 2 to 3 minutes
options.D: 5 to 10 seconds

explanation: A full 40 to 60 second duration ensures adequate mechanical friction and contact time to remove transient microbes safely. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why must a single-use towel be used to turn off the water faucet after washing?

options.A: To prevent recontaminating clean hands on a dirty tap handle
options.B: To conserve paper towel supplies by utilizing every wet section
options.C: To dry the wet faucet handle for the next healthcare worker
options.D: To polish the metallic surface and prevent bacterial growth

explanation: Faucets are touched with dirty hands before washing, so bare fingers would pick up those microbes again if used to turn off the water. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h6)

question: How long should a nurse rub hands with an alcohol-based product until dryness is achieved?

options.A: 3 to 5 minutes
options.B: 60 to 90 seconds
options.C: 5 to 10 seconds
options.D: 20 to 30 seconds

explanation: Friction must continue for 20 to 30 seconds until the alcohol completely evaporates to ensure effective pathogen destruction. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is the correct action if hands become sticky after applying an alcohol-based hand rub several times?

options.A: Apply more alcohol gel to dissolve the sticky residue
options.B: Ignore the residue until the end of the shift
options.C: Wash hands with soap and water to remove buildup
options.D: Wipe the palms dry immediately with a cloth towel

explanation: Emollient buildup from repeated gel applications requires a proper soap and water wash to clear the residue without harming skin integrity. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT allowed for clinical nurses to maintain hand hygiene safety?

options.A: Artificial fingernails
options.B: Plain metal wedding bands
options.C: Hospital-approved hand lotion
options.D: Short natural nails

explanation: Artificial nails harbor high concentrations of fungi and bacteria that resist standard hand washing and easily transfer to patients. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h8)

question: Why is occupational hand dermatitis dangerous for both the nurse and the patient?

options.A: Skin irritation stops the body from producing normal sweat
options.B: Sore hands prevent the nurse from lifting heavy equipment safely
options.C: Cracked skin harbors high bacterial loads that resist routine washing
options.D: Dermatitis makes alcohol rubs completely odorless and ineffective

explanation: Damaged skin creates microscopic fissures where pathogenic bacteria multiply beyond the reach of normal friction cleaning, increasing infection risks. [learn more](GST114_U2_T6#GST114_U2_T6_h8)

question: What breaks down organic matter in waste?

options.A: Protozoa only
options.B: Microorganisms
options.C: Inorganic salts
options.D: Synthetic polymers

explanation: Bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms naturally decompose organic components found within waste materials. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why is built-up hospital biological waste a major infection risk?

options.A: It provides a favorable environment for pathogen proliferation
options.B: It neutralizes all active chemical disinfectants
options.C: It completely stops the growth of normal flora
options.D: It converts non-hazardous waste into radioactive material

explanation: Accumulated waste supplies nutrients and moisture that allow harmful microbes to multiply rapidly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which category do used surgical blades and injection needles belong to?

options.A: Pharmaceutical waste
options.B: Sharps
options.C: Pathological waste
options.D: General waste

explanation: Items capable of causing cuts or punctures are strictly grouped as sharps to prevent injury and infection. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h2)

question: An empty plastic water bottle from a patient's bedside is what type of waste?

options.A: General waste
options.B: Infectious waste
options.C: Pathological waste
options.D: Chemical waste

explanation: Administrative and housekeeping items that have not come into contact with infectious body fluids are treated as general domestic refuse. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h2)

question: What is an infection caught by a patient while receiving hospital care called?

options.A: Idiopathic condition
options.B: Zoonotic disease
options.C: Nosocomial infection
options.D: Congenital infection

explanation: Hospital-acquired infections resulting from exposure to pathogens within a healthcare facility are known as nosocomial infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h3)

question: How do nurses most commonly get injured by waste while working?

options.A: Inhalation of dry dust particles
options.B: Absorption through intact skin
options.C: Direct ingestion of liquid reagents
options.D: Puncture wounds from contaminated needles

explanation: Improperly disposed sharps frequently cause accidental punctures, directly inoculating bloodborne pathogens into the healthcare worker. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h3)

question: When should healthcare waste be sorted into its proper bins?

options.A: During final incineration
options.B: At the point of generation
options.C: Before collection by external contractors
options.D: Inside the municipal dump site

explanation: Sorting waste immediately where it is produced prevents contamination and protects subsequent handlers. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why must sharps containers be rigid and puncture-resistant?

options.A: To keep the needles chemically sterile
options.B: To prevent accidental needle-stick injuries
options.C: To reduce the overall weight of the trash
options.D: To make the waste easier to burn

explanation: Rigid safety boxes stop sharp objects from piercing through the walls, protecting staff from accidental cuts and punctures. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h4)

question: Which waste treatment uses high-pressure steam to sterilize items?

options.A: Incineration
options.B: Open burning
options.C: Chemical burial
options.D: Autoclaving

explanation: Autoclaves utilize saturated steam under pressure to effectively destroy all microbial life on contaminated equipment and waste. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of autoclaving infectious waste instead of burning it?

options.A: It turns hazardous materials into high-grade fertilizer
options.B: It requires no electricity or external power source
options.C: It completely transforms human body parts into liquid
options.D: It avoids the release of harmful toxic smoke into the air

explanation: Steam sterilization neutralizes biological hazards without producing the heavy atmospheric pollutants associated with thermal burning. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h5)

question: Which dangerous practice with used needles must nurses avoid?

options.A: Recapping used needles
options.B: Checking fluid levels in a syringe
options.C: Transporting syringes on a tray
options.D: Dropping needles into a safety box

explanation: Attempting to recap used needles greatly increases the risk of slipping and experiencing an accidental puncture injury. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h6)

question: A nurse accidentally pokes her finger with a used needle. What is her very first step?

options.A: Apply a tight tourniquet above the elbow
options.B: Wash the site thoroughly with soap and water
options.C: Continue her ward rounds and report it at the end of the shift
options.D: Squeeze the wound hard until bleeding stops completely

explanation: Immediate washing helps remove surface contaminants and reduces the microbial load entering the puncture site. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which Nigerian federal agency enforces environmental standards and waste control?

options.A: WAEC
options.B: JAMB
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: NESREA

explanation: The National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency oversees environmental protection and waste management compliance across Nigeria. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is a major challenge for healthcare waste management in Nigerian public hospitals?

options.A: An excessive surplus of modern autoclaves in every ward
options.B: Complete absence of any infectious material in clinics
options.C: Inconsistent electricity supply required to run incinerators
options.D: Strict adherence to international laws without local input

explanation: Unreliable power infrastructure often hinders the proper operation of electrical treatment machines like incinerators and autoclaves. [learn more](GST114_U2_T7#GST114_U2_T7_h7)

question: What main feature defines a medical sharp?

options.A: Being made strictly of surgical-grade stainless steel
options.B: Containing residual hazardous chemical substances
options.C: Having sharp points or edges capable of skin penetration
options.D: Being manufactured exclusively for single-patient use

explanation: Sharps are specifically categorized by their ability to puncture or lacerate the skin due to sharp points or edges. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which item is considered a sharp in clinical practice?

options.A: Cotton wool pledget
options.B: Disposable plastic syringe barrel
options.C: Examining nitrile glove
options.D: Capillary blood lancet

explanation: Lancets are designed with a sharp point to puncture skin for blood sampling, making them high-risk sharps. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h1)

question: Which bloodborne infection has the highest risk of transmission after a single needle-stick injury?

options.A: Human immunodeficiency virus
options.B: Hepatitis C virus
options.C: Cytomegalovirus
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: Hepatitis B has a high concentration in blood and viral stability, resulting in the highest transmission rate among the common bloodborne pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why do hollow-bore needles carry a higher infection risk than solid suture needles?

options.A: They are harder to see inside tissue layers
options.B: They hold a volume of contaminated fluid inside the lumen
options.C: They are manufactured at much longer lengths
options.D: They are coated with strong chemical preservatives

explanation: Hollow-bore needles can carry and inject a reservoir of infected blood directly into the puncture wound. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h2)

question: What is the safest technique for recapping a needle if it must be done?

options.A: Using a single-handed scoop technique
options.B: Asking a colleague to hold the cap steady
options.C: Pushing the needle directly into the cap using fingers
options.D: Holding the cap firmly with the opposite hand

explanation: The single-handed scoop method keeps the non-needle hand away from the point, preventing accidental finger punctures. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h3)

question: What action should you avoid doing with used disposable needles?

options.A: Dropping them into a puncture-resistant bin
options.B: Disposing of them immediately after the injection
options.C: Bending or breaking them by hand
options.D: Carrying them on a designated treatment tray

explanation: Bending or breaking needles increases splatter risk and accidental finger lacerations. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h3)

question: At what fill level should a sharps container be closed and replaced?

options.A: Three-quarters full
options.B: One-quarter full
options.C: Half full
options.D: Completely packed to the brim

explanation: Replacing containers at three-quarters capacity prevents protruding items from causing punctures during disposal and sealing. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h4)

question: Where should a sharps container ideally be placed in a patient ward?

options.A: High up on a wall shelf out of general reach
options.B: Inside a locked utility room at the end of the corridor
options.C: At eye level and within arm's reach near the point of use
options.D: On the floor underneath the medication preparation trolley

explanation: Placing the container near the point of use avoids dangerous transit of uncapped sharps across busy clinical spaces. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h4)

question: What is the first thing a nurse should do after a needle-stick injury?

options.A: Search for the patient's laboratory file results
options.B: Complete an official incident report form for management
options.C: Wash the puncture site with running water and soap
options.D: Squeeze the wound hard to force out contaminated blood

explanation: Washing the wound immediately helps remove surface contaminants and reduce pathogen load before seeking medical evaluation. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why is squeezing or massaging a needle-stick wound discouraged?

options.A: It violates standard institutional incident reporting protocols
options.B: It causes excessive bleeding that is difficult to stop on the ward
options.C: It delays the administration of the routine tetanus toxoid booster
options.D: It can damage local tissues and drive pathogens deeper into blood vessels

explanation: Massaging or squeezing the puncture site increases local micro-trauma and can push infectious agents further into the bloodstream. [learn more](GST114_U2_T8#GST114_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of the cleaning stage in decontamination?

options.A: To remove visible organic matter and dirt
options.B: To apply chemical preservatives to metal surfaces
options.C: To destroy all bacterial spores on the device
options.D: To lower the temperature of hot instruments

explanation: Cleaning physically removes blood, tissue, and dirt using water and detergents, which must happen before disinfection or sterilization can work properly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h1)

question: Why is cleaning considered mandatory before performing disinfection or sterilization?

options.A: Dried organic matter shields microorganisms from chemical agents
options.B: Detergents double as high-level sterilizing agents
options.C: Washing instruments reduces their overall weight in storage
options.D: Chemical disinfectants react dangerously with wet steel surfaces

explanation: Residual blood and protein act as a physical barrier that prevents heat or chemicals from reaching the underlying pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h1)

question: A blood pressure cuff touches intact skin only, placing it in which Spaulding category?

options.A: Sterile item
options.B: Critical item
options.C: Non-critical item
options.D: Semi-critical item

explanation: Items that contact only intact skin require low-level disinfection and are classified as non-critical. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h2)

question: What level of processing is required for medical devices classified as semi-critical?

options.A: Absolute sterilization
options.B: Low-level disinfection
options.C: High-level disinfection
options.D: Simple washing with soap and water

explanation: Semi-critical items touch mucous membranes and require the destruction of all microorganisms except high numbers of bacterial spores. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h2)

question: Which physical method is considered the most reliable for routine instrument sterilization in hospitals?

options.A: Boiling water in a standard pot
options.B: Cold water immersion soaking
options.C: Steam sterilization under pressure
options.D: Ultraviolet radiation exposure

explanation: Autoclaving uses moist heat under pressure to ensure complete destruction of spores and all other microbes. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h3)

question: A nurse needs to reprocess heat-stable surgical forceps. Which decontamination method should be selected?

options.A: Autoclaving
options.B: Low-temperature soaking
options.C: Sun drying
options.D: Alcohol wiping

explanation: Surgical forceps are critical items made of heat-stable metal, making steam autoclaving the gold standard choice. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary clinical difference between a disinfectant and an antiseptic?

options.A: Disinfectants are used on inanimate objects, while antiseptics are used on living tissue
options.B: Disinfectants require heat activation, while antiseptics work instantly at room temperature
options.C: Antiseptics kill bacterial spores, while disinfectants only kill fungi
options.D: Antiseptics are restricted to surgical theatres, while disinfectants are for home use only

explanation: The safety profile of antiseptics allows them to be applied safely to human skin and wounds, unlike harsher chemical disinfectants. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h4)

question: Why must endoscopes processed in glutaraldehyde undergo thorough rinsing with sterile water before reuse?

options.A: To cool down the internal camera mechanism
options.B: To ensure the metal coils do not rust prematurely
options.C: To reactivate the drying properties of the scope lens
options.D: To prevent chemical irritation of patient tissues

explanation: Residual glutaraldehyde is toxic to mucous membranes and can cause severe inflammation or burns if introduced into the body. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the first operational step in the instrument decontamination workflow immediately following a clinical procedure?

options.A: Point of use removal of gross debris
options.B: Immediate packaging in paper pouches
options.C: Soaking in pure alcohol solution
options.D: Placement in the high-pressure autoclave

explanation: Wiping off gross soil right after use stops organic material from drying and hardening onto the instrument surface. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why must the decontamination workflow always move in one direction from dirty to clean areas?

options.A: To speed up the drying time of washed surgical trays
options.B: To reduce the electricity consumed by automated washers
options.C: To comply with fire safety codes in hospital basements
options.D: To prevent the recontamination of sterile or processed items

explanation: A unidirectional workflow separates contaminated equipment from clean supplies, stopping pathogenic spread within the processing unit. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h5)

question: Which item of personal protective equipment is essential when manually washing contaminated surgical instruments?

options.A: Sterile surgical gown and latex examination gloves
options.B: Lead apron and waterproof rubber boots
options.C: Heavy-duty utility gloves and a face shield
options.D: N95 respirator mask and cloth head covering

explanation: Washing instruments creates splashing risks that require waterproof protection for the hands, face, and eyes against biological and chemical hazards. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h6)

question: What is the correct action to take regarding used injection needles during instrument cleanup?

options.A: Dispose of them directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container without recapping
options.B: Break the needle tip off with pliers to eliminate accidental pricks
options.C: Recap them carefully using a two-handed technique before placing them on a tray
options.D: Soak them in bleach solution overnight alongside metal scissors

explanation: Recapping needles is a leading cause of needlestick injuries and should never be performed; dispose of them unrecapped immediately. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h6)

question: What do biological indicators use to test the efficacy of a steam sterilization cycle?

options.A: Highly resistant bacterial endospores
options.B: Electronic temperature and pressure sensors
options.C: Heat-sensitive chemical dye strips
options.D: Visible blood residue on test plates

explanation: Biological indicators contain actual spores that are very hard to kill, providing the ultimate proof that the sterilizer works properly. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h7)

question: A nurse opens an autoclave pack and notices the chemical indicator strip failed to change color. What action is required?

options.A: Wipe the instruments with alcohol and use them anyway
options.B: Place the strip in direct sunlight to activate the dye
options.C: Treat the instruments as unsterile and reprocess them
options.D: Use a permanent marker to change the color manually

explanation: A failed chemical indicator means the required processing parameters were not met, so the instruments cannot be considered sterile for patient use. [learn more](GST114_U2_T9#GST114_U2_T9_h7)

question: What is another common name for normal flora in the human body?

options.A: Sterile contaminants
options.B: Pathogenic invaders
options.C: Indigenous microbiota
options.D: Parasitic protozoa

explanation: Normal flora are frequently referred to as indigenous microbiota because they naturally reside within specific host tissues. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h1)

question: How do commensal microbes interact with their human host?

options.A: Both the host and microbe gain mutual benefits
options.B: The microbe benefits without harming the host
options.C: The host benefits while the microbe dies
options.D: Both the microbe and host suffer damage

explanation: Commensalism describes a biological relationship where one organism gains an advantage while the other remains unaffected. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h1)

question: Which type of microbiota stays on the skin for only a short period?

options.A: Pathogenic microbiota
options.B: Transient microbiota
options.C: Mutualistic microbiota
options.D: Resident microbiota

explanation: Transient microbes are picked up from the environment and only linger temporarily on human skin. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h2)

question: Why do transient microbes eventually disappear from human skin?

options.A: They require constant reinfection to survive
options.B: They fail to compete with resident flora
options.C: They burrow deep into subcutaneous tissues
options.D: They transform into permanent resident flora

explanation: Resident microbes occupy receptor sites and consume available nutrients, making it difficult for transient visitors to survive long-term. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h2)

question: Which bacterial species is most commonly found colonizing the healthy human skin?

options.A: Clostridium botulinum
options.B: Staphylococcus epidermidis
options.C: Neisseria meningitidis
options.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a major resident microbe thriving on the dry, salty surface of human skin. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h3)

question: What is the primary role of vaginal Lactobacillus species in healthy adult females?

options.A: Producing nutrients for uterine wall growth
options.B: Maintaining an acidic pH to block pathogens
options.C: Stimulating active labor contractions
options.D: Preventing normal hormonal fluctuations

explanation: Lactobacillus ferments glycogen to lactic acid, creating an acidic environment that prevents harmful bacteria and fungi from overgrowing. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h3)

question: When does the initial acquisition of normal flora in humans primarily begin?

options.A: Around the age of three
options.B: At the time of weaning
options.C: During the process of birth
options.D: During early puberty

explanation: Infants acquire their first major exposure to microbes as they pass through the birth canal or encounter environmental touch after delivery. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h4)

question: How does breastfeeding influence the infant gut microbiome compared to formula feeding?

options.A: It introduces harsh pathogens into the stomach
options.B: It keeps the infant's digestive tract completely sterile
options.C: It encourages the dominance of Bifidobacteria
options.D: It eliminates all bacteria from the large intestine

explanation: Breast milk contains specific oligosaccharides that selectively feed and promote the growth of beneficial Bifidobacteria in the infant gut. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which essential vitamin is synthesized by normal flora in the human gut?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Vitamin K
options.C: Vitamin D
options.D: Vitamin A

explanation: Intestinal microbes play a vital role in producing Vitamin K, which is necessary for proper blood clotting. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary protective mechanism known as microbial antagonism?

options.A: The immune system clearing out all beneficial microbes
options.B: Resident flora blocking pathogens from gaining resources
options.C: Microbes actively attacking the host's white blood cells
options.D: Pathogens destroying the body's normal resident bacteria

explanation: Microbial antagonism occurs when established flora take up all available attachment sites and nutrients, preventing harmful invaders from taking hold. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h5)

question: What term describes a harmless resident microbe that causes disease when host defenses fail?

options.A: Primary pathogen
options.B: Opportunistic pathogen
options.C: Obligate parasite
options.D: Transient contaminant

explanation: Opportunistic pathogens take advantage of a weakened immune system or altered body environment to cause disease. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why does broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy sometimes lead to secondary fungal or bacterial overgrowth?

options.A: It permanently converts human tissue cells into foreign bacterial cells
options.B: It destroys protective normal flora that kept competing microbes in check
options.C: It shuts down the production of all white blood cells in the bone marrow
options.D: It directly stimulates the rapid growth of pathogenic viral strains

explanation: Wiping out beneficial resident bacteria removes microbial antagonism, allowing opportunistic organisms to multiply unchecked. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the single most effective nursing action to prevent the spread of transient microbiota?

options.A: Applying sterile ointments daily
options.B: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.C: Isolating every patient in a private room
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics

explanation: Handwashing removes transient microorganisms acquired from environmental contact, stopping transmission between patients. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why must a nurse follow strict aseptic technique when inserting a urinary catheter?

options.A: To stimulate the growth of beneficial resident bacteria
options.B: To avoid pushing skin flora into the sterile bladder
options.C: To ensure the catheter tubing remains clear of mucus
options.D: To prevent the patient from developing skin allergies

explanation: Invasive devices like catheters can easily carry surface microbes into normally sterile internal organs, causing infection. [learn more](GST114_U3_T1#GST114_U3_T1_h7)

question: What makes a pathogen different from other microbes?

options.A: It causes disease in a susceptible host
options.B: It can only be seen with an electron microscope
options.C: It lacks genetic material for reproduction
options.D: It lives exclusively in water environments

explanation: Pathogens are microbes that can overcome body defenses and cause illness. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is learning about pathogens important for nursing practice?

options.A: It helps predict disease spread and guide prevention
options.B: It ensures patients never develop chronic illnesses
options.C: It allows nurses to manufacture synthetic antibiotics
options.D: It eliminates the need for routine hand hygiene

explanation: Knowing how germs spread helps nurses stop infections before they start. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h1)

question: What is a main structural difference between fungi and bacteria?

options.A: Bacteria lack any form of cellular membrane
options.B: Bacteria are classified exclusively as multicellular parasites
options.C: Fungi possess rigid cell walls made of chitin
options.D: Fungi contain nuclear material within a true nucleus

explanation: Fungi have a true nucleus, making them eukaryotes, while bacteria are simpler prokaryotes without a true nucleus. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why do viruses need a living host cell to multiply?

options.A: They depend on sunlight to activate their protein coats
options.B: They lack the cellular machinery needed for replication
options.C: They feed directly on red blood cells for energy
options.D: They dissolve instantly in free-standing water supplies

explanation: Viruses cannot copy themselves on their own, so they take over a host cell's machinery to reproduce. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h2)

question: Malaria spreading through female Anopheles mosquitoes is an example of what kind of transmission?

options.A: Vector-borne transmission
options.B: Direct contact spread
options.C: Vehicle-borne transmission
options.D: Airborne transmission

explanation: Vectors like mosquitoes carry and pass infectious agents from one person to another. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which nursing action helps stop infection at the portal of entry?

options.A: Administering broad-spectrum oral vitamins daily
options.B: Spraying chemical disinfectants on hospital walls
options.C: Using proper aseptic technique and wound dressings
