options.D: Isolating infected patients in private hospital rooms

explanation: Sterile dressings and clean techniques create a barrier that keeps germs out of the body. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h3)

question: During which stage of an infection do clear signs and symptoms first show up?

options.A: Illness stage
options.B: Incubation period
options.C: Convalescent period
options.D: Prodromal stage

explanation: The illness stage is when the germ population peaks and classic signs of the disease appear. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why is the incubation period a challenge for controlling disease outbreaks?

options.A: Diagnostic laboratories cannot detect any pathogens in the blood
options.B: Pathogens are completely inactive and produce no toxins yet
options.C: Infected individuals feel well and spread the microbe unknowingly
options.D: Immune systems stop functioning during this phase entirely

explanation: People without symptoms usually go about their normal day, spreading the germ without knowing it. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the main goal of a culture and sensitivity test?

options.A: To measure the exact white blood cell count in serum
options.B: To count the number of antibodies produced by the spleen
options.C: To determine which antimicrobial drugs can kill the pathogen
options.D: To calculate the incubation period of a viral infection

explanation: Sensitivity tests check which drugs work best against a specific germ. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h5)

question: Why must a nurse collect lab specimens carefully?

options.A: To ensure the laboratory technician processes it faster
options.B: To prevent contamination from normal flora on the skin
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of running blood panels
options.D: To eliminate the need for patient consent documentation

explanation: Avoiding skin germs on the sample prevents false results and wrong treatments. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h5)

question: What practice is a major cause of antimicrobial resistance?

options.A: Incomplete courses and misuse of antimicrobial drugs
options.B: Proper sterilization of surgical instruments after use
options.C: Rigorous adherence to standard handwashing protocols
options.D: Isolating patients with confirmed drug-resistant infections

explanation: Stopping medication early allows stronger germs to survive and build resistance. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why is it important for patients to finish their entire course of antibiotics?

options.A: It speeds up the normal tissue healing cycle in wounds
options.B: It prevents the patient from developing chronic allergies
options.C: It reduces the financial burden on local pharmacies
options.D: It ensures all resilient pathogens are completely eradicated

explanation: Stopping drugs when feeling better can leave tougher bacteria behind, leading to a relapse. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which nursing action is the single most effective way to prevent spreading infections?

options.A: Administering prophylactic vitamins
options.B: Changing bed linens twice daily
options.C: Regular and thorough hand hygiene
options.D: Wearing sterile gowns during meals

explanation: Washing hands removes transient germs picked up from patient care, stopping cross-infection. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h7)

question: When should a nurse use airborne precautions for a patient?

options.A: When large respiratory droplets travel less than one meter
options.B: When the pathogen is spread via tiny suspended droplet nuclei
options.C: When bloodborne viruses are detected in laboratory results
options.D: When the patient has an infection spread strictly by direct touch

explanation: Airborne precautions use special masks and rooms for tiny germs that float in the air. [learn more](GST114_U3_T2#GST114_U3_T2_h7)

question: What primary role do microorganisms play in natural aquatic ecosystems?

options.A: Producing pure chemical compounds for industry
options.B: Breaking down organic waste in nutrient cycles
options.C: Creating physical barriers against aquatic plants
options.D: Eliminating all dissolved oxygen from the water

explanation: Aquatic microbes act as natural decomposers that recycle nutrients and break down organic matter in water bodies. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why is the study of water microbiology essential for nursing practice?

options.A: It trains nurses to manufacture chemical water filters
options.B: It replaces the need for standard hospital sterilization protocols
options.C: It allows nurses to diagnose rare tropical skin parasites
options.D: It helps prevent the community spread of water-borne diseases

explanation: Nurses must understand how pathogens travel through water supplies to effectively educate communities on disease prevention. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which microbial group is primarily responsible for photosynthesis near the water surface?

options.A: Pathogenic viral spores
options.B: Deep-sea heterotrophic fungi
options.C: Transient sewage bacteria
options.D: Algae and cyanobacteria

explanation: Cyanobacteria and algae contain chlorophyll to capture sunlight for energy and oxygen production near the water surface. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h2)

question: What does the term 'allochthonous flora' mean when describing a natural water body?

options.A: Native bacteria that permanently colonize the deep sediment
options.B: Photosynthetic organisms that produce native river oxygen
options.C: Genetically modified microbes added for water purification
options.D: Microbes washed in from external sources like soil or sewage

explanation: Allochthonous microorganisms originate outside the water body and enter via runoff, rain, or wastewater discharge. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h2)

question: An industrial pipe discharging untreated waste directly into a river is an example of what?

options.A: Natural mineral leaching
options.B: Point source pollution
options.C: Non-point source pollution
options.D: Autochthonous contamination

explanation: Point source pollution comes from a single, identifiable, and localized discharge point like a pipe or drain. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h3)

question: A community experiences a sudden rise in water contamination following heavy rains washing fertilizer and animal waste from nearby farms. What type of pollution is this?

options.A: Controlled municipal runoff
options.B: Point source industrial pollution
options.C: Internal microbial proliferation
options.D: Non-point source pollution

explanation: Agricultural runoff enters water bodies from diffuse, broad areas rather than a single pipe, making it non-point pollution. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h3)

question: Which organism is the causative agent of cholera?

options.A: Vibrio cholerae
options.B: Entamoeba histolytica
options.C: Salmonella typhi
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Cholera is a severe diarrheal disease caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae spreading through contaminated water. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h4)

question: A patient presents with severe watery diarrhea and rapid dehydration after drinking untreated river water. Which disease is most likely?

options.A: Malaria
options.B: Hepatitis A
options.C: Tuberculosis
options.D: Cholera

explanation: Massive watery diarrhea leading to rapid dehydration is the classic clinical presentation of cholera infection. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h4)

question: Why are indicator organisms used in water quality testing instead of screening for every pathogen?

options.A: Pathogens cannot survive long enough in a laboratory container
options.B: Testing for every specific pathogen is impractical and slow
options.C: Indicator bacteria give exact chemical measurements of heavy metals
options.D: Indicator organisms destroy all other harmful bacteria in the sample

explanation: Screening water for hundreds of different potential pathogens is too difficult, so reliable indicator bacteria are used instead. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h5)

question: What does the presence of Escherichia coli in a drinking water sample indicate?

options.A: The water has undergone successful chemical chlorination
options.B: Recent faecal contamination from human or animal waste
options.C: High levels of harmless photosynthetic aquatic algae
options.D: Natural mineral enrichment of deep underground aquifers

explanation: E. coli lives in the gut, so finding it in water proves that faecal matter has entered the supply. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h5)

question: Which stage of water treatment involves adding chemicals to form heavy flocs from suspended particles?

options.A: Charcoal bed filtration
options.B: Sedimentation basin resting
options.C: Terminal chlorination
options.D: Coagulation and flocculation

explanation: Coagulation and flocculation use binding chemicals to cause tiny suspended particles to clump together into heavier masses. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of disinfection in municipal water treatment plants?

options.A: To settle heavy dirt particles to the bottom of the tank
options.B: To remove unpleasant odors caused by decaying plants
options.C: To adjust the overall mineral balance and pH of the water
options.D: To destroy remaining pathogenic bacteria and viruses

explanation: Disinfection is the final pathogen-killing step utilizing chlorine, ozone, or UV radiation to ensure microbiological safety. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is a key nursing intervention for preventing water-borne infections in rural Nigerian communities with poor infrastructure?

options.A: Constructing large municipal chlorination plants in every village
options.B: Prescribing prophylactic antibiotics to all healthy community members
options.C: Prohibiting the use of local boreholes without chemical testing
options.D: Educating residents on household water purification methods like boiling

explanation: When municipal systems are absent, teaching practical home water treatment empowers communities to protect themselves. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h7)

question: A public health nurse is deployed to a community experiencing a sudden cholera outbreak. Which activity should be prioritized?

options.A: Distribution of industrial chemical solvents to households
options.B: Collection of soil samples for agricultural parasite testing
options.C: Active disease surveillance and community health education
options.D: Immediate closure of all local hospitals and clinics

explanation: During an outbreak, tracking cases and teaching prevention methods are crucial nursing duties to halt transmission. [learn more](GST114_U3_T3#GST114_U3_T3_h7)

question: What primary feature makes milk an excellent growth medium for microorganisms?

options.A: Extremely high acidic pH level
options.B: High concentration of natural antibiotics
options.C: Rich supply of essential nutrients
options.D: Complete absence of water content

explanation: Milk provides water, proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates that microorganisms need to multiply quickly. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h1)

question: Freshly expressed milk from a healthy cow contains which type of natural protective factors?

options.A: Strong digestive enzymes
options.B: Active live vaccines
options.C: Synthetic preservatives
options.D: Antimicrobial substances

explanation: Proteins like lactoferrin and lysozyme naturally inhibit early bacterial growth in raw milk. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h1)

question: Fecal matter and soil on the cow udder primarily introduce which type of contaminant into milk?

options.A: Internal mammary viruses
options.B: Pure synthetic chemicals
options.C: Modified plant proteins
options.D: External environmental bacteria

explanation: Dirt and manure on the outer udder surface easily fall into the milk pail or machine during milking. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h2)

question: Poorly washed milking equipment causes high bacterial counts mainly by harboring what formation?

options.A: Beneficial yeast spores
options.B: Resistant bacterial biofilms
options.C: Sterile mineral deposits
options.D: Protective enzyme layers

explanation: Inadequately cleaned pipes and tanks allow bacteria to stick and form protective layers that resist simple rinsing. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which bacteria found in unpasteurized milk causes brucellosis in humans?

options.A: Brucella species
options.B: Acetobacter aceti
options.C: Streptococcus thermophilus
options.D: Lactobacillus acidophilus

explanation: Brucella bacteria are zoonotic pathogens transmitted directly through unpasteurized milk and dairy products. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why is relying on sensory checks alone dangerous for detecting pathogens in raw milk?

options.A: Pathogens often do not change milk appearance or smell
options.B: Pathogens cause milk to turn bright green immediately
options.C: Fresh milk naturally smells like chemical disinfectants
options.D: Spoilage bacteria always destroy pathogenic microbes first

explanation: Dangerous bacteria can multiply to high levels without altering the visual or olfactory qualities of the milk. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which disease is classically transmitted to humans through drinking infected, unpasteurized cow milk?

options.A: Bovine tuberculosis
options.B: Bacterial tetanus
options.C: Viral hepatitis C
options.D: Plasmodium malaria

explanation: Mycobacterium bovis infects cattle and passes into milk, causing tuberculosis in humans who drink it raw. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which demographic group faces the highest health risk from drinking raw, unpasteurized milk?

options.A: Experienced livestock farmers
options.B: Active middle-aged athletes
options.C: Young children and pregnant women
options.D: Healthy adult industrial workers

explanation: Immune systems in children and pregnant women are more susceptible to severe complications from foodborne pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the standard time and temperature for High-Temperature Short-Time (HTST) pasteurization?

options.A: 100°C for 60 seconds
options.B: 72°C for 15 seconds
options.C: 135°C for 3 seconds
options.D: 63°C for 30 minutes

explanation: HTST uses 72°C for 15 seconds to rapidly destroy pathogens in a continuous commercial flow. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h5)

question: How does UHT sterilization differ fundamentally from standard pasteurization methods?

options.A: It maintains live beneficial bacteria in the carton
options.B: It requires constant refrigeration after packaging
options.C: It uses chemical additives instead of thermal energy
options.D: It destroys bacterial spores for ambient storage

explanation: Ultra-high temperatures eliminate all spores, allowing shelf-stable storage without refrigeration until opened. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h5)

question: The presence of coliform bacteria in pasteurized milk typically indicates what type of issue?

options.A: Natural vitamin enrichment
options.B: High protein concentration
options.C: Optimal refrigeration storage
options.D: Post-pasteurization contamination

explanation: Coliforms are destroyed by proper heat treatment, so their presence reveals recontamination after processing. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h6)

question: What does a methylene blue reduction test measure in a sample of raw milk?

options.A: Exact percentage of milk fat content
options.B: Presence of added synthetic water
options.C: Total concentration of dissolved calcium
options.D: Metabolic activity of living bacteria

explanation: Active bacteria consume oxygen and change the color of the dye, indicating bacterial load and freshness. [learn more](GST114_U3_T4#GST114_U3_T4_h6)

question: What primary group of microorganisms is studied in food microbiology alongside bacteria and viruses?

options.A: Protozoa and plants
options.B: Algae and amphibians
options.C: Helminths and worms
options.D: Yeasts and molds

explanation: Yeasts and molds are major fungal groups heavily involved in food fermentation and spoilage alongside bacteria. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why is studying food microbiology vital for clinical nursing practice in local communities?

options.A: It helps nurses prevent water and food-borne illnesses through education.
options.B: It enables nurses to cure chronic genetic food allergies.
options.C: It teaches nurses how to chemically treat infected crop farms.
options.D: It allows nurses to manufacture commercial antibiotics in hospitals.

explanation: Knowledge of foodborne pathogens enables nurses to guide patients on proper hygiene and safe food preparation. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which organism type is primarily responsible for fermenting local staples like ogi and fufu?

options.A: Lactic acid bacteria
options.B: Pathogenic salmonella
options.C: Photosynthetic protozoa
options.D: Sporing anaerobic fungi

explanation: Lactic acid bacteria ferment carbohydrates in staples like ogi, producing acids that preserve the food. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h2)

question: How do beneficial bacteria prevent the growth of harmful pathogens in fermented foods?

options.A: By releasing toxic heavy metals into the food matrix
options.B: By lowering pH through the production of organic acids
options.C: By consuming all the available moisture in the container
options.D: By raising the internal temperature above boiling point

explanation: Acid production creates an acidic environment that inhibits the survival of most disease-causing bacteria. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h2)

question: What class of compounds do bacteria typically produce when spoiling protein-rich foods like meat?

options.A: Nucleic acids
options.B: Amines
options.C: Simple sugars
options.D: Complex starches

explanation: The breakdown of proteins by bacteria releases foul-smelling volatile amines, causing the characteristic odor of rotting meat. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h3)

question: Which food type is most commonly attacked by molds and yeasts rather than bacteria?

options.A: Salted marine fish fillets
options.B: High-carbohydrate or acidic foods
options.C: Boiled eggs kept at room temperature
options.D: Freshly slaughtered raw beef

explanation: Molds and yeasts tolerate acidic environments and lower moisture levels better than most bacteria, making fruits and baked goods prime targets. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h3)

question: What is the temperature range known as the danger zone where bacteria multiply rapidly?

options.B: 5°C to 60°C
options.C: Minus 10°C to 0°C
options.D: 0°C to 10°C

explanation: The temperature danger zone permits rapid bacterial proliferation in perishable foods left unprotected. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why does adding high concentrations of salt or sugar preserve food effectively?

options.A: It lowers water activity and dehydrates microbial cells.
options.B: It neutralizes the natural pH to make the food sterile.
options.C: It introduces oxygen molecules that poison anaerobic bacteria.
options.D: It raises the internal temperature to kill spores instantly.

explanation: High solute concentrations draw water out of microbial cells via osmosis, stopping their metabolic activity. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h4)

question: What distinguishes a food-borne intoxication from a food-borne infection?

options.A: Infections are caused exclusively by viral chemical contaminants.
options.B: Intoxications require live bacteria to colonize the intestinal wall.
options.C: Infections never present with vomiting or abdominal cramps.
options.D: Intoxications are caused by ingesting pre-formed microbial toxins.

explanation: Food intoxication happens when toxins produced by bacteria grow in the food and are eaten, even if the bacteria are dead. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h5)

question: A patient presents with acute watery diarrhea and severe dehydration after eating improperly stored custard. What underlying process is most likely responsible?

options.A: Rapid chemical fermentation of dietary fiber
options.B: Cellular destruction by ingested fungal spores
options.C: Bacterial multiplication and toxin ingestion
options.D: Immediate immune rejection of food proteins

explanation: Custard is a protein-rich medium where bacteria like Staphylococcus easily multiply and release heat-stable enterotoxins. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which preservation process uses controlled heat to reduce pathogenic bacteria in liquids like milk?

options.A: Pasteurization
options.B: Salinization
options.C: Lyophilization
options.D: Fermentation

explanation: Pasteurization heats liquids to specific temperatures for set times to kill harmful pathogens without ruining the food quality. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h6)

question: Why is separating raw and cooked foods a critical food safety practice?

options.A: It prevents the physical mixing of distinct flavors and food aromas.
options.B: It ensures that cooked food retains its essential mineral and vitamin contents.
options.C: It stops the natural chemical fermentation process inside storage containers.
options.D: It prevents cross-contamination of pathogens from raw items to ready-to-eat food.

explanation: Raw items often carry harmful bacteria that can easily transfer to cooked food via unwashed hands, knives, or cutting boards. [learn more](GST114_U3_T5#GST114_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is another name for nematodes?

options.A: Pinworms
options.B: Flukes
options.C: Roundworms
options.D: Tapeworms

explanation: Nematodes are cylindrical, unsegmented parasites commonly called roundworms. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h1)

question: How do tapeworms (cestodes) get their food inside a human host?

options.A: Absorbing nutrients directly through their skin
options.B: Feeding exclusively on red blood cells
options.C: Digesting food particles via a complete gut
options.D: Ingesting host blood using sharp suckers

explanation: Tapeworms do not have a digestive tract, so they absorb nutrients directly through their outer skin from the host's intestines. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h1)

question: How do hookworm larvae usually enter the human body?

options.A: Eating poorly cooked fish
options.B: Active penetration of bare skin
options.C: Mosquito bites
options.D: Breathing in dust particles

explanation: Hookworm larvae live in contaminated soil and can burrow directly through human skin, usually when people walk barefoot. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which blood cell type usually increases during a parasite infection?

options.A: Erythrocytes
options.B: Leukocytes
options.C: Eosinophils
options.D: Thrombocytes

explanation: When parasites invade tissues, the body triggers an immune response that raises the number of circulating eosinophils. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h2)

question: What health problem is most commonly caused by a heavy, long-term hookworm infection?

options.A: Kidney failure
options.B: Intestinal blockage
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Respiratory failure

explanation: Hookworms feed on blood in the intestines, which leads to chronic blood loss and iron deficiency anemia. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h3)

question: How do people usually catch schistosomiasis in rural communities?

options.A: Wading in stagnant freshwater bodies
options.B: Inhaling dust from farm soil
options.C: Eating undercooked beef or pork
options.D: Drinking unpasteurized milk

explanation: Parasite larvae come out of freshwater snails and penetrate the skin of people who swim, wash, or farm in infested water. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is a common physical sign in a patient with a heavy Ascaris (roundworm) infection?

options.A: Swollen legs
options.B: Abdominal distension
options.C: Skin jaundice
options.D: A stiff neck

explanation: Large bundles of roundworms can build up in the intestines, causing the abdomen to look and feel swollen. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which symptom is typical of a pinworm infection?

options.A: Nighttime itching around the anus
options.B: Painful leg swelling
options.C: Swollen neck glands
options.D: Right upper belly pain

explanation: Female pinworms crawl out of the rectum at night to lay eggs around the anus, causing intense itching. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h4)

question: What is the main laboratory test used to diagnose intestinal worms?

options.A: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
options.B: Blood glucose test
options.C: Sputum culture
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis

explanation: Looking at stool samples under a microscope helps find worm eggs or larvae. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h5)

question: A nurse suspects urinary schistosomiasis in a patient with blood in their urine. Which sample should be collected?

options.A: Rectal swab
options.B: Fasting blood draw
options.C: Midday terminal urine sample
options.D: 24-hour sputum collection

explanation: Schistosoma haematobium eggs are best collected near the end of urination around midday when bladder pressure is highest. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h5)

question: How do deworming drugs like albendazole kill intestinal worms?

options.A: Stopping the formation of cell structures in the worm
options.B: Destroying the outer protective skin
options.C: Blocking nerve signals in the muscles
options.D: Causing severe dehydration

explanation: Benzimidazoles disrupt cell building blocks in worms, stopping them from absorbing glucose so they starve. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h6)

question: Which medication is specifically used to treat schistosomiasis and tapeworms?

options.A: Metronidazole
options.B: Praziquantel
options.C: Benzylpenicillin
options.D: Gentamicin

explanation: Praziquantel makes parasite cell walls more permeable to calcium, which paralyzes flukes and tapeworms. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is the main focus of patient education after treatment for worms?

options.A: Eating a high-protein diet
options.B: Restricting fluid intake
options.C: Preventing reinfection through good hygiene
options.D: Avoiding exercise for two weeks

explanation: Teaching handwashing, wearing shoes, and properly washing food stops patients from getting infected all over again. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h7)

question: A community nurse is preparing for a school deworming program. What is the main action to take?

options.A: Giving scheduled deworming tablets to the pupils
options.B: Doing stool tests on every single student
options.C: Prescribing iron supplements for all parents
options.D: Isolating infected children

explanation: Mass drug administration in schools involves giving safe, single-dose deworming tablets to lower the total worm burden in the community. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h7)

question: Which public health measure has the biggest long-term impact on reducing soil-transmitted worms?

options.A: Mandatory annual chest x-rays
options.B: Isolating infected patients
options.C: Spraying chemicals on farmlands
options.D: Improving sanitation and safe toilets

explanation: Proper sanitation stops human waste from mixing with the soil, which cuts off the transmission cycle at the source. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h8)

question: What is the main goal of mass deworming programs in primary schools?

options.A: Treating surgical emergencies
options.B: Reducing overall worm load and illness
options.C: Eradicating all parasites worldwide
options.D: Diagnosing rare blood disorders

explanation: Treating groups of children lowers parasite levels, preventing severe illness and nutritional problems. [learn more](GST114_U3_T6#GST114_U3_T6_h8)

question: What developmental stage comes immediately after the egg stage in insects undergoing complete metamorphosis?

options.A: Pupa
options.B: Adult
options.C: Nymph
options.D: Larva

explanation: The larval stage follows the egg in complete metamorphosis, serving primarily as the active feeding and growth phase before pupation. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why is the larval stage important when controlling vector-borne diseases?

options.A: It is resistant to all insecticides
options.B: It is the final reproductive stage
options.C: It infects human blood directly
options.D: It is the main feeding phase where targeted interventions work well

explanation: Targeting vectors during their localized larval development is often more effective than chasing mobile adult insects. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h1)

question: What name is given to the successive developmental moulting phases of growing larvae?

options.A: Scolices
options.B: Cysts
options.C: Instars
options.D: Spiracles

explanation: Larvae grow by shedding their outer cuticle multiple times, with each phase between moults referred to as an instar. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the main biological function of the larval stage in most insects?

options.A: Feeding and growing rapidly
options.B: Hibernating
options.C: Spreading pollen
options.D: Laying eggs

explanation: Larvae dedicate almost all their energy to consuming nutrients and growing larger to prepare for metamorphosis. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h2)

question: The tumbu fly larva which infests human skin is an example of what condition?

options.A: Myiasis
options.B: Malaria
options.C: Filariasis
options.D: Schistosomiasis

explanation: Myiasis is the infestation of live human or animal tissue by fly larvae. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h3)

question: A patient presents with itchy skin lesions on the feet after walking barefoot on damp soil. Which larval type is responsible?

options.A: Mosquito wigglers
options.B: Fly maggots
options.C: Mite larvae
options.D: Soil-transmitted helminth larvae

explanation: Hookworm and Strongyloides larvae live in contaminated soil and actively penetrate bare human skin. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h3)

question: What skin lesion is produced by migrating animal hookworm larvae in cutaneous larva migrans?

options.A: Serpiginous and itchy tunnels
options.B: Painless hard nodules
options.C: Fluid-filled blisters
options.D: Dry scaly patches

explanation: As the larvae crawl through the outer skin layers, they leave behind raised, winding, intensely itchy tracks. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h4)

question: Why do furuncular myiasis skin lesions maintain a small central opening?

options.A: To apply antiseptic creams
options.B: To prevent fungal infections
options.C: To let the larva breathe air
options.D: To allow white blood cells to drain

explanation: The burrowing maggot positions its breathing tubes near the skin opening to breathe while feeding underneath. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h4)

question: Spreading damp clothing on the ground in humid areas can cause infestation by which insect larva?

options.A: Sand fly
options.B: Tumbu fly
options.C: House fly
options.D: Tse-tse fly

explanation: Female tumbu flies lay eggs on soil or damp clothing spread outside, and the hatching larvae penetrate skin when garments are worn. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h5)

question: Which group faces the highest risk of contracting cutaneous larval infections from contaminated soil?

options.A: Laboratory scientists
options.B: Children and farmers walking barefoot
options.C: Office workers
options.D: Fishermen

explanation: Direct skin contact with soil contaminated by animal feces puts barefoot individuals at high risk of larval penetration. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h5)

question: What blood test finding is most commonly associated with tissue-invading parasitic larvae?

options.A: Neutropenia
options.B: Eosinophilia
options.C: Thrombocytosis
options.D: Polycythemia

explanation: Tissue invasion by parasites typically triggers an elevated white blood cell count dominated by eosinophils. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of taking a detailed travel history when parasitic larvae are suspected?

options.A: To determine the organism's genetics
options.B: To identify the likely source of environmental exposure
options.C: To calculate the exact incubation period
options.D: To assess the patient's finances

explanation: Knowing where a patient walked or slept helps pinpoint whether the vector originated from soil, clothes, or water. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h6)

question: Applying petroleum jelly to a furuncular myiasis lesion forces the trapped larva to do what?

options.A: Dissolve
options.B: Migrate deeper
options.C: Surface for air
options.D: Lay more eggs

explanation: Blocking the breathing pore with ointment suffocates the maggot, forcing it to crawl out where it can be extracted safely. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h7)

question: Why should you avoid crushing a fly maggot while pulling it out of a skin lesion?

options.A: It damages nerve endings permanently
options.B: It triggers a severe local inflammatory reaction
options.C: It causes the larva to multiply
options.D: It releases infectious viruses

explanation: Leaving larval fragments or body fluids inside the wound provokes intense inflammation and secondary bacterial infection. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h7)

question: What household practice effectively kills tumbu fly eggs hidden in damp laundry?

options.A: Soaking in cold salty water
options.B: Starching garments
options.C: Ironing with a hot iron
options.D: Drying in the shade

explanation: High heat from a hot pressing iron destroys any fly eggs or newly hatched larvae lingering in fabric folds. [learn more](GST114_U3_T7#GST114_U3_T7_h8)

question: How do community sanitation programs help reduce vector-borne larval threats?

question: What biological structure do parasitic ova represent?

question: What is the primary route of transmission for soil-transmitted helminth ova?

options.C: Ingestion of contaminated food or water

question: Which organ damage is commonly associated with tissue-trapped Schistosoma ova?

question: How do heavy burdens of intestinal parasite ova indirectly affect pediatric patients?

options.C: By causing permanent neurological paralysis
options.D: By causing malnutrition and growth stunting

question: What is the primary purpose of stool concentration techniques in parasitology?

question: A nurse collects a stool specimen for ova and parasite testing. What action ensures accurate test results?

question: Which public health intervention directly reduces the spread of soil-transmitted ova?

question: What is the primary function of the human immune system?

question: Why is self-nonself discrimination important for the immune system?

options.B: To increase white blood cell production during stress

options.D: To attack foreign invaders while sparing healthy host tissues

explanation: Self-nonself discrimination is the crucial ability of immune cells to recognize native body tissues and avoid attacking them while targeting foreign invaders. [learn more](GST114_U4_T1#GST114_U4_T1_h1)

question: Which feature makes the adaptive immune response different from innate immunity?

question: Where do T lymphocytes primarily mature in the human body?

question: What is the main job of secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes?

question: Where are MHC Class I molecules normally found in the body?

question: Which cells show MHC Class II molecules to interact with helper T cells?

question: Anaphylaxis from a severe peanut allergy is an example of which hypersensitivity type?

question: How do secondary immunodeficiencies differ from primary immunodeficiencies?

options.D: Secondary immunodeficiencies are acquired later in life due to external factors

question: What type of immunity is given by receiving ready-made antibodies?

options.C: Herd immunity
options.D: Active immunity

question: How do standard vaccines create long-term protection against infections?

options.C: By replacing damaged white blood cells in bone marrow

question: What common laboratory test uses enzyme-labeled antibodies to find specific antigens?

question: A nurse is preparing to draw blood for an immune test. What is the most important action?

question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is serum sickness?

question: Which common treatment is a well-known trigger for serum sickness in clinical practice?

question: How do non-protein drugs like penicillin sometimes cause a reaction similar to serum sickness?

question: Which symptom is almost always present in patients with serum sickness?

question: Why is a urine test (urinalysis) important when checking for serum sickness?

question: What is the very first step in managing a patient with suspected serum sickness?

question: When are systemic corticosteroids usually prescribed for serum sickness?

options.C: For severe cases with systemic symptoms and organ involvement

question: Which nursing action helps relieve joint discomfort in a patient with serum sickness?

question: What is a crucial piece of advice a nurse must give a recovering serum sickness patient before discharge?

question: What is the usual outlook (prognosis) for someone diagnosed with serum sickness?

question: What is the main difference between acquired and congenital immune deficiencies?

question: Why are patients with weak immune systems in big danger from everyday germs?

options.C: Their red blood cell count drops and starves tissues

question: Which specific cells are mainly attacked as HIV infection gets worse?

question: What happens directly when the body loses T-helper cell function?

question: At what CD4 cell count does an HIV infection officially progress to AIDS?

question: An HIV-positive patient shows no symptoms for several years. What is this phase called?

question: How does severe malnutrition directly weaken the body's immune defenses?

question: Which common childhood illness can cause temporary immune amnesia?

question: What is a major medical treatment cause of bone marrow suppression during cancer care?

question: Why do organ transplant patients need ongoing care to suppress their immune systems?

question: Which diagnostic test counts the exact number of T-helper cells in a patient's blood?

question: A patient comes in with white patches in the mouth and a long-lasting fever. What health issue should a nurse think of first?

question: What is the main reason healthcare workers must wash their hands carefully around patients with weak immune systems?

question: Which food safety rule is most important for a patient with a very weak immune system?

question: What does PMTCT stand for in public health programs?

question: Why are community health nurses so important in managing immune deficiencies in Nigeria?

question: What is the main job of an antigen in the body?
