explanation: Antigens are foreign substances that the immune system recognizes, prompting it to produce antibodies. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why are complex proteins usually better antigens than simple lipids?

options.A: Proteins have more complex and varied structures for immune recognition
options.B: Lipids cannot enter the bloodstream under any circumstances
options.C: Proteins destroy white blood cells before they react
options.D: Simple lipids dissolve completely in body fluids instantly

explanation: Varied structural shapes allow immune cells to easily spot and bind to protein antigens compared to simpler molecules. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h1)

question: What do we call the ability of a substance to provoke an immune response?

options.A: Pathogenicity
options.B: Immunogenicity
options.C: Virulence
options.D: Cytotoxicity

explanation: Immunogenicity is the specific term for a substance's capacity to cause an immune reaction in the body. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h2)

question: A small medication particle fails to trigger an immune reaction. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The molecular size is too small to be immunogenic
options.B: The chemical structure is too complex for lymphocytes
options.C: The substance has high foreignness value
options.D: The medication acts directly as a superantigen

explanation: Very small molecules lack the size needed to stimulate the immune system on their own. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which type of antigen comes from outside the body, such as bacteria and pollen?

options.A: Exogenous antigens
options.B: Endogenous antigens
options.C: Autoantigens
options.D: Alloantigens

explanation: Exogenous antigens originate outside the body and are captured by specialized immune cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why are ABO blood group markers classified as alloantigens?

options.A: They are produced inside host cells during viral replication
options.B: They always originate from bacterial infections in the gut
options.C: They vary among different individuals of the same species
options.D: They trigger autoimmune destruction of red blood cells

explanation: Alloantigens are genetic differences found between people of the same species, making blood matching crucial for transfusions. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is another name for an antigenic determinant?

options.A: Hapten
options.B: Alloantigen
options.C: Superantigen
options.D: Epitope

explanation: An epitope is the specific part of an antigen that antibodies or immune receptors attach to. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h4)

question: How can one large antigen molecule stimulate several different immune reactions at once?

options.A: It prevents white blood cells from communicating
options.B: It breaks down into harmless inert carbon molecules
options.C: It contains multiple distinct epitopes on its surface
options.D: It duplicates its genetic material inside host tissues

explanation: Large antigens have many binding sites on their surface, allowing different immune cells to target the same invader. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the main characteristic of a hapten by itself?

options.A: It is always a large complex protein molecule
options.B: It directly activates T-cells without processing
options.C: It lacks immunogenicity without a carrier
options.D: It originates only from internal cell metabolism

explanation: Haptens are tiny molecules that need to attach to a larger carrier protein before they can trigger an immune response. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h5)

question: A patient has an allergic reaction because penicillin binds to body proteins. What is penicillin called in this situation?

options.A: Superantigen
options.B: Autoantigen
options.C: Alloantigen
options.D: Hapten

explanation: Penicillin acts as a hapten by linking up with larger proteins in the body to set off an immune reaction. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which type of antigen needs help from T-helper cells to activate B-cells?

options.A: T-independent antigens
options.B: T-dependent antigens
options.C: Hapten carriers
options.D: Autoantigens

explanation: T-dependent antigens require helper T-cells to fully activate B-cells and build lasting immune memory. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is a key feature of how the body responds to T-independent antigens?

options.A: They fail to trigger any observable immune reaction
options.B: They consist exclusively of large globular proteins
options.C: They primarily produce IgM antibodies with limited memory
options.D: They require complex processing by antigen-presenting cells

explanation: T-independent antigens activate B-cells directly, which leads to quick IgM antibody release but very little long-term memory. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h6)

question: What makes superantigens much more dangerous than regular antigens?

options.A: They reduce inflammation to dangerously low levels
options.B: They block the production of all antibodies in the body
options.C: They completely destroy all circulating red blood cells
options.D: They activate a massive percentage of T-cells simultaneously

explanation: Superantigens bypass normal checks and activate a huge number of T-cells at the same time, causing a dangerous chemical flood. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why does a superantigen reaction often result in systemic shock?

options.A: Normal antibodies bind to haptens and block blood flow
options.B: T-cells consume all available oxygen in the bloodstream
options.C: The body stops producing white blood cells entirely
options.D: Uncontrolled massive cytokine release damages multiple organ systems

explanation: An overwhelming release of inflammatory proteins causes blood vessels to dilate dangerously, leading to shock. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h7)

question: A patient having a blood transfusion suddenly gets a fever, chills, and back pain. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Autoimmune tolerance
options.B: Hapten protein binding
options.C: Superantigen release
options.D: Alloantigen mismatch

explanation: Transfusion reactions happen when the donor's blood cells have alloantigens that the patient's antibodies attack. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h8)

question: Why do nurses need to understand antigens when learning about vaccines?

options.A: It ensures that patients never develop minor injection site pain
options.B: It prevents medications from acting as dangerous haptens
options.C: It guarantees complete immunity against all bacterial strains
options.D: It helps explain how safe, weakened antigens stimulate long-term immunity

explanation: Vaccines use harmless parts of antigens to safely teach the immune system how to fight off future diseases. [learn more](GST114_U4_T2#GST114_U4_T2_h8)

question: What type of cells in the body produce antibodies?

options.A: Plasma cells
options.B: Platelets
options.C: Fibroblasts
options.D: Erythrocytes

explanation: Plasma cells develop from activated B-lymphocytes and specialize in synthesizing and secreting large volumes of immunoglobulins. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h1)

question: What is the main role of immunoglobulins (antibodies) in the body?

options.A: Digest dietary proteins
options.B: Produce red blood cells
options.C: Transport oxygen gas
options.D: Neutralize foreign antigens

explanation: Antibodies circulate in body fluids to specifically target, bind, and neutralize foreign invaders like bacteria and viruses. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which part of an antibody molecule binds directly to an antigen?

options.A: Heavy chain base
options.B: Complement stem
options.C: Fc region
options.D: Fab region

explanation: The Fab region contains the variable amino acid sequences responsible for specific antigen recognition and binding. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the basic shape and structure of a standard antibody unit?

options.A: A globular cluster of light chains only
options.B: A circular ring with four heavy chains
options.C: A linear chain with five variable regions
options.D: A Y-shape with two heavy and two light chains

explanation: Standard antibody monomers consist of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains arranged in a characteristic Y shape. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h2)

question: Which antibody class is primarily found in mucosal secretions like saliva and breast milk?

options.A: IgA
options.B: IgG
options.C: IgE
options.D: IgD

explanation: Secretory IgA is abundant in mucosal linings, tears, saliva, and colostrum to guard the body's entry points against pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is IgM effective as the first responder during an infection?

options.A: It forms a large structure with many binding sites
options.B: It is stored in high concentrations inside skin cells
options.C: It is the smallest antibody and crosses tissue barriers easily
options.D: It binds exclusively to red blood cell membranes

explanation: IgM typically circulates as a pentamer containing ten antigen-binding sites, making it exceptionally effective at clumping early invaders. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the process called when antibodies coat a pathogen to enhance phagocytosis?

options.A: Opsonization
options.B: Agglutination
options.C: Neutralization
options.D: Transcription

explanation: Opsonization labels foreign particles with antibodies or complement proteins so phagocytes can easily spot and ingest them. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h4)

question: How does antibody neutralization protect host cells from viral infections?

options.A: By blocking the virus from attaching to host cell receptors
options.B: By signaling red blood cells to absorb the viral particles
options.C: By increasing body temperature to destroy the pathogen
options.D: By dissolving the outer protein coat of the virus directly

explanation: Neutralizing antibodies physically cover viral attachment sites, stopping the virus from entering and infecting healthy cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which cell type is responsible for the rapid antibody production seen in a repeat (secondary) immune response?

options.A: Epithelial cells
options.B: Platelet reserves
options.C: Neutrophil precursors
options.D: Memory B-cells

explanation: Memory B-cells survive for long periods after an initial infection, ready to divide rapidly upon re-exposure to the same antigen. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why is the secondary immune response much faster than the primary response?

options.A: The body already possesses specialized memory cells ready to react
options.B: First-time exposure completely exhausts the immune system
options.C: Pathogens move slower the second time they enter the body
options.D: The liver releases stored antibodies directly into the bloodstream

explanation: Pre-existing memory cells bypass the lengthy lag phase required to prime naive lymphocytes during a primary exposure. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h5)

question: Finding high levels of specific IgM antibodies in a patient's blood sample usually indicates...

options.A: complete absence of white blood cells
options.B: a chronic long-term genetic disorder
options.C: immunity from a childhood vaccination
options.D: a recent or current acute infection

explanation: IgM is the primary antibody produced during the initial phase of an immune response, signaling a fresh or active infection. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h6)

question: How are monoclonal antibodies generally used in modern medical treatments?

options.A: As targeted therapies to attack specific cancer cells
options.B: As broad-spectrum painkillers for severe joint injuries
options.C: As dietary supplements to boost daily energy levels
options.D: As replacement fluids for severe dehydration cases

explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are engineered in labs to lock onto specific target proteins, such as markers found on tumor cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T3#GST114_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is another name for non-specific body defences?

options.A: Specific immunity
options.B: Acquired immunity
options.C: Innate immunity
options.D: Adaptive immunity

explanation: Innate immunity refers to the body's natural, non-specific defenses present from birth. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why are non-specific defences considered rapid compared to adaptive immunity?

options.A: They only target viruses within the bloodstream
options.B: They do not require prior exposure to pathogens
options.C: They depend on T-lymphocyte maturation in the thymus
options.D: They rely on antibody production by plasma cells

explanation: Because innate defences react uniformly to all invaders without needing time to recognize specific antigens, they mount a fast response. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h1)

question: What structure in the respiratory tract moves trapped mucus upward?

options.A: Villi
options.B: Cilia
options.C: Nephrons
options.D: Alveoli

explanation: Respiratory cilia beat rhythmically to propel mucus and trapped pathogens away from the lungs. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h2)

question: A burn patient loses large areas of skin. Which immune function is primarily compromised?

options.A: The production of specific antibodies against bacteria
options.B: The physical barrier against microbial entry
options.C: The maturation of cytotoxic T-lymphocytes
options.D: The activation of the complement cascade system

explanation: Intact skin serves as the primary structural barrier of the first line of defence, preventing external pathogens from entering. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h2)

question: Where is the enzyme lysozyme commonly found to help destroy bacteria?

options.A: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Bile and pancreatic fluid
options.C: Gastric juice
options.D: Tears and saliva

explanation: Lysozyme is present in body fluids like tears and saliva, where it breaks down bacterial cell walls. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h3)

question: How does stomach acid protect the gastrointestinal tract from infection?

options.A: It stimulates the production of specific viral antibodies
options.B: It coats the mucosal surface with a protective mucus layer
options.C: It creates a low pH environment that destroys ingested pathogens
options.D: It activates resident neutrophils in the stomach lining

explanation: The highly acidic environment of the stomach denatures proteins and kills most swallowed microbes. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h3)

question: Which white blood cells are the most abundant and arrive first at an infection site?

options.A: Basophils
options.B: Neutrophils
options.C: Lymphocytes
options.D: Eosinophils

explanation: Neutrophils circulate in high numbers and are the primary responders to acute bacterial infections. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h4)

question: What is the primary function of Natural Killer (NK) cells?

options.A: Destroying virus-infected and tumor cells
options.B: Secreting hydrochloric acid in the stomach
options.C: Producing specific antibodies for bacterial antigens
options.D: Phagocytosing large cellular debris in tissues

explanation: Natural killer cells target abnormal host cells, such as those infected by viruses or transformed into cancer. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h4)

question: Which chemical mediator is released by mast cells to cause vasodilation during inflammation?

options.A: Amylase
options.B: Thyroxine
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Histamine

explanation: Mast cells release histamine, which dilates blood vessels and increases capillary permeability during the inflammatory response. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h5)

question: What causes the localized swelling seen during acute inflammation?

options.A: Accumulation of red blood cells trapped by constricted veins
options.B: Contraction of skeletal muscle fibers near the injury site
options.C: Rapid replication of resident bacteria in the wound bed
options.D: Fluid leaking from permeable capillaries into interstitial tissues

explanation: Increased capillary permeability allows plasma and proteins to escape into the tissue spaces, resulting in edema or swelling. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h5)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat to regulate fever?

options.A: Hypothalamus
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Thalamus

explanation: The hypothalamus controls body temperature and resets the thermal set point when pyrogens are present. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h6)

question: How does a moderate fever help the body fight off an infection?

options.A: It slows down the growth rate of many pathogens
options.B: It stops the production of endogenous pyrogens
options.C: It destroys healthy tissue to create a barrier
options.D: It prevents white blood cells from entering the blood

explanation: Higher body temperatures inhibit the replication of various bacteria and viruses while boosting immune cell efficiency. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC) in the complement system?

options.A: Punching holes in target cell membranes to cause lysis
options.B: Sweeping mucus upward in the respiratory tract
options.C: Stimulating the hypothalamus to raise body temperature
options.D: Secreting histamine from localized mast cells

explanation: The MAC forms pores in pathogen cell membranes, leading to fluid influx and cell destruction. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h7)

question: How do interferons protect uninfected cells during a viral illness?

options.A: They form a physical waxy coating over mucous membranes
options.B: They directly phagocytose free-floating viral particles
options.C: They prompt neighboring cells to produce virus-blocking enzymes
options.D: They neutralize viral toxins released into the bloodstream

explanation: Interferons act as warning signals, prompting nearby healthy cells to synthesize proteins that interfere with viral replication. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h7)

question: A nurse inserts an indwelling urinary catheter. Which innate defense mechanism is primarily bypassed?

options.A: The chemical action of gastric acid in the stomach
options.B: The physical barrier of the urogenital mucous membranes
options.C: The systemic pyrogenic control of the hypothalamus
options.D: The cellular activity of circulating neutrophils

explanation: Urinary catheters cross mucosal barriers, creating a direct pathway for bacteria into the urinary tract. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h8)

question: A patient with an intravenous cannula shows local redness, warmth, and swelling at the insertion site. What physiological process explains these findings?

options.A: Localized inflammatory response causing vasodilation and fluid leakage
options.B: Systemic immune failure requiring immediate antipyretic administration
options.C: Interferon release halting viral replication in adjacent skin cells
options.D: Activation of the complement cascade leading to membrane attack

explanation: Redness, heat, and swelling are cardinal signs of localized inflammation driven by increased blood flow and capillary permeability. [learn more](GST114_U4_T4#GST114_U4_T4_h8)

question: What is another name for specific body defences?

options.A: Inflammatory response
options.B: Innate immunity
options.C: Adaptive immunity
options.D: Mechanical barrier

explanation: Specific body defences are also referred to as adaptive or acquired immunity because they target specific pathogens. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h1)

question: The primary feature that separates adaptive immunity from innate immunity is its ability to do what?

options.A: Target specific foreign invaders
options.B: Trigger non-specific inflammation
options.C: Prevent entry through the skin
options.D: Act immediately upon exposure

explanation: Adaptive immunity tailors its response to particular pathogens rather than providing a generalized defence. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h1)

question: What is the specific region on an antigen that binds to an immune receptor?

options.A: Pathogen
options.B: Antibody
options.C: Hapten
options.D: Epitope

explanation: An epitope is the specific molecular site on an antigen that is recognized by immune cells and antibodies. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why do small molecules known as haptens need carrier proteins to trigger an immune response?

options.A: They inhibit the normal function of primary lymphoid organs
options.B: They are too small to provoke an immune reaction on their own
options.C: They immediately neutralize circulating white blood cells
options.D: They destroy carrier proteins before antibodies can form

explanation: Haptens lack sufficient molecular size to be immunogenic by themselves until attached to a larger carrier molecule. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h2)

question: Where do T-lymphocytes mature in the human body?

options.A: Bone marrow
options.B: Thymus
options.C: Lymph node
options.D: Spleen

explanation: T-cells originate in the bone marrow but travel to the thymus gland to complete their maturation process. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h3)

question: A patient has an infection trapped in the regional lymph nodes. What is the main function of these organs here?

options.A: To destroy all circulating platelets in the bloodstream
options.B: To produce naive T-cells from immature stem cells
options.C: To manufacture red blood cells for oxygen transport
options.D: To filter antigens and help activate lymphocytes

explanation: Secondary lymphoid organs trap foreign particles and provide a meeting place for antigens and mature immune cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which type of cell develops from activated B-cells to release large amounts of antibodies?

options.A: Helper T-cell
options.B: Erythrocyte
options.C: Neutrophil
options.D: Plasma cell

explanation: Plasma cells are specialized effector B-cells dedicated to producing and releasing massive quantities of antibodies. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary role of memory B-cells formed during an initial infection?

options.A: To replace damaged tissue in primary lymphoid organs
options.B: To provide a faster and stronger response upon re-exposure
options.C: To produce non-specific inflammatory chemicals immediately
options.D: To actively engulf extracellular bacteria in the bloodstream

explanation: Memory B-cells persist long-term to recognize subsequent invasions of the same antigen and mount a swift defense. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h4)

question: Which T-cell subset is primarily responsible for directly destroying virus-infected host cells?

options.A: Plasma cells
options.B: Memory B-cells
options.C: Helper T-cells
options.D: Cytotoxic T-cells

explanation: Cytotoxic T-cells identify cells bearing intracellular pathogens and induce cell destruction. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why must T-cells rely on antigen-presenting cells to detect foreign invaders?

options.A: They cannot recognize free-floating antigens directly
options.B: They destroy any cell that lacks MHC molecules
options.C: They lack receptors capable of binding to protein epitopes
options.D: They only function inside the primary lymphoid organs

explanation: T-cells require antigens to be processed and presented on MHC molecules by other cells before activation can occur. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h5)

question: What part of an antibody molecule binds directly to an antigen?

options.A: Fc region
options.B: Fab region
options.C: Heavy chain stem
options.D: Complement protein

explanation: The variable tips of the Y-shaped antibody, known as the Fab region, form the specific antigen-binding site. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h6)

question: How does opsonization assist the immune system in clearing a bacterial infection?

options.A: By coating the bacteria to make phagocytosis easier
options.B: By neutralizing circulating toxins released by microbes
options.C: By directly lysing the bacterial cell wall without cells
options.D: By preventing pathogens from attaching to host tissues

explanation: Opsonization tags pathogens with antibodies, marking them for efficient engulfment and destruction by phagocytic cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h6)

question: What type of immunity is gained when an infant receives antibodies through breast milk?

options.A: Artificial active immunity
options.B: Natural active immunity
options.C: Natural passive immunity
options.D: Artificial passive immunity

explanation: Breast milk transfers maternal antibodies directly to the infant, providing natural passive protection without immune activation. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is a major limitation of passive immunization compared to active vaccination?

options.A: It causes severe allergic reactions in every patient
options.B: It does not stimulate the production of memory cells
options.C: It only protects against intracellular viral infections
options.D: It takes several weeks to begin offering any protection

explanation: Because passive immunity supplies ready-made antibodies rather than provoking the host's own response, protection is temporary. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h7)

question: What accounts for the rapid and robust response during a secondary exposure to an antigen?

options.A: Inflammatory chemicals
options.B: Innate barrier proteins
options.C: Memory cells
options.D: Primary neutrophils

explanation: Memory cells left behind from the first exposure allow the immune system to react much faster and stronger the next time. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h8)

question: How do standard vaccines safely prepare the body to fight off dangerous infectious diseases?

options.A: By supplying temporary antibodies that last for a few weeks
options.B: By introducing harmless antigens to stimulate memory cell formation
options.C: By destroying primary lymphoid organs to prevent severe infections
options.D: By replacing all naive T-cells with artificial immune cells

explanation: Vaccines safely expose the immune system to non-virulent antigen forms, prompting the generation of protective memory cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T5#GST114_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary function of the human immune system?

options.A: Defending the body against pathogens
options.B: Producing red blood cells
options.C: Regulating blood pressure levels
options.D: Filtering waste from urine

explanation: The primary role of the immune system is to protect the body from harmful foreign invaders and diseases. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h1)

question: Why are skin and mucous membranes considered part of the immune defense?

options.A: They act as physical barriers blocking entry
options.B: They destroy old red blood cells directly
options.C: They digest food particles for energy
options.D: They produce antibodies inside the blood

explanation: External barriers prevent pathogens from entering the body tissues in the first place. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which type of immunity is present from birth?

options.A: Innate immunity
options.B: Artificial immunity
options.C: Passive immunity
options.D: Adaptive immunity

explanation: Innate immunity is non-specific and present at birth to provide immediate baseline protection. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h2)

question: What makes adaptive immunity different from innate immunity?

options.A: It relies solely on skin and mucous membranes
options.B: It acts immediately within the first few minutes
options.C: It targets specific pathogens and creates memory
options.D: It remains identical throughout a person's life

explanation: Adaptive immunity builds specific responses to individual germs and remembers them for future encounters. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h2)

question: How is natural active immunity typically acquired?

options.A: Surviving a natural infection
options.B: Receiving an infant vaccine
options.C: Receiving a blood transfusion
options.D: Getting antibodies from breast milk

explanation: Natural active immunity develops when an individual gets sick and recovers, prompting their own immune system to fight back. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h3)

question: Why does artificial active immunity through vaccination provide long-term protection?

options.A: It provides ready-made antibodies that circulate permanently
options.B: It permanently alters the person's genetic code
options.C: It stimulates memory cell creation without causing severe disease
options.D: It destroys all pathogens entering the body forever

explanation: Vaccines safely teach the immune system to recognize antigens and form lasting memory cells. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h3)

question: What is the main characteristic of passive immunity?

options.A: It requires the body to manufacture its own defense cells
options.B: It takes several weeks to start producing antibodies
options.C: It provides temporary protection because memory cells are absent
options.D: It lasts for the entire lifetime of the individual

explanation: Passive immunity supplies ready-made antibodies that eventually degrade, offering short-term relief without lasting memory. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h4)

question: An infant receiving maternal antibodies through breast milk is an example of what type of immunity?

options.A: Artificial active immunity
options.B: Artificial passive immunity
options.C: Natural passive immunity
options.D: Natural active immunity

explanation: Passing antibodies from mother to child naturally without the child's immune system working for it is natural passive immunity. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h4)

question: Which cells are primarily responsible for humoral immunity?

options.A: Platelets
options.B: T lymphocytes
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: B lymphocytes

explanation: B cells mature into plasma cells that secrete antibodies into body fluids during humoral responses. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary target of cell-mediated immunity?

options.A: Dust particles trapped inside nasal passages
options.B: Foreign toxins dissolved in digestive juices
options.C: Free-floating bacteria in the blood plasma
options.D: Cells infected by viruses or abnormal cancer cells

explanation: T cells handle intracellular threats by targeting and destroying host cells that harbor viruses or turn abnormal. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h5)

question: A nurse caring for a patient receiving immunosuppressant drugs should prioritize which nursing action?

options.A: Enforcing strict hand hygiene and infection prevention protocols
options.B: Administering live vaccines to boost active immunity immediately
options.C: Encouraging heavy contact with large crowds to stimulate cells
options.D: Withholding all oral medications to protect the digestive tract

explanation: Immunocompromised patients lack effective defenses, making rigorous infection control critical for their survival. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h6)

question: Why is checking a patient's immunization record important in clinical practice?

options.A: To determine if they have inherited genetic blood disorders
options.B: To calculate the correct dosage of daily intravenous fluids
options.C: To evaluate their status regarding artificial active immunity
options.D: To measure the exact level of red blood cells present

explanation: Immunization records reveal whether a patient has received necessary vaccines to build artificial active immunity. [learn more](GST114_U4_T6#GST114_U4_T6_h6)

question: What are the three main categories of immune system dysregulation?

options.A: Phagocytosis, inflammation, and complement activation
options.B: Innate, adaptive, and acquired immunity
options.C: Hypersensitivity, autoimmunity, and immunodeficiency
options.D: Antibody production, cellular destruction, and lysis

explanation: Immune system dysregulation typically manifests as overactive responses, attacks on self-tissues, or a complete lack of immune response. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h1)

question: Why is immune system balance critical for human health?

options.A: It stops the production of red blood cells
options.B: It ensures all white blood cells reproduce rapidly
options.C: It increases the body temperature to kill bacteria
options.D: It prevents both tissue destruction and severe infections

explanation: A balanced immune system fights off pathogens without attacking the body or failing to respond when needed. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which hypersensitivity type is mediated by IgE and causes immediate anaphylaxis?

options.A: Type III
options.B: Type IV
options.C: Type I
options.D: Type II

explanation: Type I reactions involve IgE binding to mast cells, causing rapid histamine release and allergic symptoms. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h2)

question: A positive tuberculin skin test after 48 hours is an example of which hypersensitivity reaction?

options.A: Type IV
options.B: Type II
options.C: Type III
options.D: Type I

explanation: Delayed-type hypersensitivity is mediated by T cells rather than antibodies, taking days to show visible inflammation. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary underlying problem in autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Loss of self-tolerance by the immune system
options.B: Overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: Complete absence of white blood cells
options.D: Permanent blockage of the lymphatic vessels

explanation: Autoimmunity happens when the body stops recognizing its own tissues as safe and attacks them. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h3)

question: Which factor commonly interacts with genetics to trigger autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Excessive physical exercise and muscle strain
options.B: Environmental triggers such as viral infections
options.C: Eating a high-protein diet during childhood
options.D: Lack of exposure to clean drinking water

explanation: Infections and other environmental factors can trigger autoimmune responses in genetically susceptible individuals. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h3)

question: What distinguishes primary immunodeficiencies from secondary immunodeficiencies?

options.A: Secondary deficiencies cannot be managed with drugs
options.B: Secondary deficiencies only affect red blood cells
options.C: Primary deficiencies are caused by viral infections
options.D: Primary deficiencies are inherited genetic defects

explanation: Primary immune disorders are present from birth due to genetic mutations, unlike acquired secondary forms. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h4)

question: A patient develops an immunodeficiency years after contracting HIV. How is this classified?

options.A: Type I hypersensitivity
options.B: Primary immunodeficiency
options.C: Autoimmune disorder
options.D: Secondary immunodeficiency

explanation: Conditions acquired after birth, such as HIV or malnutrition, are classified as secondary immunodeficiencies. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h4)

question: What specific markers does the recipient's immune system check on transplanted tissues?

options.A: Human leukocyte antigens
options.B: Complement protein receptors
options.C: Red blood cell antigens
options.D: Platelet aggregation factors

explanation: HLAs are the main target for the recipient immune system during graft rejection. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h5)

question: Why do transplant recipients need lifelong immunosuppressive medications?

options.A: To stimulate rapid healing of the surgical incision
options.B: To cure any underlying chronic infections in the body
options.C: To stop the production of red blood cells temporarily
options.D: To prevent their immune system from rejecting the organ

explanation: Immunosuppressants lower the body's ability to attack foreign donor tissue, keeping the graft safe. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h5)

question: Which blood test panel is commonly ordered when screening for autoimmune diseases?

options.A: Antinuclear antibody panel
options.B: Complete blood count alone
options.C: Liver function enzyme test
options.D: Basic metabolic electrolyte panel

explanation: Autoantibody tests, such as the antinuclear antibody (ANA) panel, help detect immune attacks against self-tissues. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of checking a complete blood count with differential in immune disorders?

options.A: To check for elevated levels of blood glucose
options.B: To assess the levels of specific white blood cell subsets
options.C: To measure the exact clotting time of the blood
options.D: To determine the total volume of blood in the body

explanation: The differential part of the CBC shows counts for neutrophils, lymphocytes, and other cells vital for immunity. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h6)

question: A patient with a severe immunodeficiency is admitted to the ward. Which nursing action is most critical?

options.A: Implementing strict infection control and hand hygiene
options.B: Administering high doses of live attenuated vaccines
options.C: Placing the patient on a high-sodium restriction diet
options.D: Encouraging frequent visitors to support recovery

explanation: Immunodeficient patients have low defense systems, making rigorous infection prevention vital for safety. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h7)

question: What is a primary responsibility when caring for patients taking immunosuppressive drugs?

options.A: Encouraging heavy physical exercise daily
options.B: Checking blood pressure every fifteen minutes
options.C: Restricting all fluid intake to prevent swelling
options.D: Monitoring closely for early signs of hidden infection

explanation: Immunosuppressants increase infection risk, so nurses must watch closely for subtle signs of sepsis or illness. [learn more](GST114_U4_T7#GST114_U4_T7_h7)

question: What term describes the normal immune system ability to ignore healthy host tissues?

options.A: Autoimmunity
options.B: Hypersensitivity
options.C: Immunodeficiency
options.D: Self-tolerance

explanation: Self-tolerance refers to the immune system capacity to recognize self antigens and refrain from attacking normal body tissues. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why does the body normally eliminate autoreactive lymphocytes during development?

options.A: To enhance defense against viral infections
options.B: To stimulate antibody production in the spleen
options.C: To increase the production of red blood cells
options.D: To prevent attacks on healthy host tissues

explanation: Deleting or inactivating autoreactive cells stops the immune system from mistakenly targeting the body own organs. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h1)

question: What mechanism occurs when a pathogen shares structural similarities with host proteins?

options.A: Bystander activation
options.B: Molecular mimicry
options.C: Antibody suppression
options.D: Cryptic antigen exposure

explanation: Molecular mimicry happens when immune cells targeting a similar microbial structure mistakenly attack healthy body tissues. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h2)

question: A patient develops an autoimmune reaction after tissue trauma exposes hidden cellular proteins. What process explains this?

options.A: Lymphocyte proliferation
options.B: Cryptic antigen exposure
options.C: Passive immunity transfer
options.D: Active immunization

explanation: Internal cell components that are normally hidden from immune surveillance can trigger a response if released during trauma. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h2)

question: Which genetic markers are frequently linked to a strong predisposition for autoimmune disorders?

options.A: Coagulation factor genes
options.B: Human leukocyte antigens
options.C: Platelet membrane receptors
options.D: Red blood cell antigens

explanation: Specific human leukocyte antigen variants alter how antigens are presented to T-cells, increasing autoimmune risk. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h3)

question: Why do environmental triggers alone rarely cause autoimmune disease in everyone exposed to them?

options.A: The liver quickly neutralizes all environmental toxins before exposure
options.B: Infections always build permanent immunity without side effects
options.C: Red blood cells absorb the environmental triggers instantly
options.D: Genetic susceptibility is also required for the disease to manifest

explanation: Autoimmunity usually requires both an underlying genetic risk and an environmental spark to break tolerance. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h3)

question: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is classified as which type of autoimmune condition?

options.A: Organ-specific
options.B: Systemic
options.C: Hypersensitive
options.D: Immunodeficient

explanation: Type 1 diabetes specifically targets insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas rather than widespread body tissues. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h4)

question: Systemic lupus erythematosus differs from organ-specific diseases because it primarily affects which structure?

options.A: Only the functional cells of the liver
options.B: Multiple organ systems and connective tissues
options.C: Just the inner lining of the stomach
options.D: Exclusively the peripheral nerve endings

explanation: Systemic diseases involve widespread autoantibody production that damages multiple organs throughout the body. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h4)

question: What common blood test screens for widespread autoimmune activity by detecting antibodies against cell nuclei?

options.A: Antinuclear antibody test
options.B: Liver function panel
options.C: Basic metabolic panel
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: The antinuclear antibody test checks for autoantibodies that bind to contents of the cell nucleus, common in systemic diseases. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h5)

question: Why do nurses monitor inflammatory markers like ESR and CRP in patients with suspected autoimmunity?

options.A: To measure the exact number of circulating red blood cells
options.B: To evaluate the presence and severity of systemic inflammation
options.C: To determine the patient dietary intake of proteins
options.D: To calculate the patient daily fluid balance

explanation: ESR and CRP levels rise during active inflammatory and autoimmune processes in the body. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of teaching energy conservation techniques to a patient with an autoimmune disease?

options.A: Preventing sudden rises in systemic blood pressure
options.B: Reducing the need for regular anti-inflammatory medications
options.C: Helping the patient manage chronic fatigue during daily tasks
options.D: Stimulating appetite to prevent severe weight loss

explanation: Energy conservation helps patients pace themselves and reserve strength when dealing with persistent fatigue. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h6)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of chronic autoimmune flare-ups requiring careful nursing pacing?

options.A: Severe hypoglycemia
options.B: Sudden visual loss
options.C: Uncontrolled bleeding
options.D: Debilitating fatigue

explanation: Persistent and overwhelming fatigue is a hallmark feature reported by individuals managing autoimmune disorders. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h6)

question: Which drug class is commonly used to rapidly suppress inflammation during an acute autoimmune flare-up?

options.A: Antibiotics
options.B: Corticosteroids
options.C: Diuretics
options.D: Antivirals

explanation: Corticosteroids act quickly to reduce widespread inflammation and curb aggressive immune activity. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h7)

question: Why must nurses closely monitor patients taking long-term immunosuppressive drugs for autoimmune disorders?

options.A: To check for signs of improved kidney filtration speed
options.B: To detect early signs of opportunistic infections
options.C: To prevent sudden drops in red blood sugar levels
options.D: To assess for the development of severe hypertension

explanation: Suppressing the immune system leaves the body vulnerable to infections that a healthy immune system normally fights off. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h7)

question: What is a major reason why patients with long-term autoimmune conditions face an elevated risk of cardiovascular disease?

options.A: Daily physical exercise becomes entirely impossible for them
options.B: Patients completely stop eating healthy foods after diagnosis
options.C: Blood pressure always drops to dangerous levels permanently
options.D: Persistent systemic inflammation damages blood vessels over time

explanation: Ongoing inflammatory processes contribute to vascular damage and plaque buildup, increasing cardiac risks. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h8)

question: What is NOT a typical goal of long-term care in chronic autoimmune conditions?

options.A: Monitoring for adverse effects of immunosuppressants
options.B: Achieving a complete permanent cure within weeks
options.C: Preventing irreversible damage to vital body organs
options.D: Coordinating multidisciplinary patient follow-up

explanation: Most autoimmune diseases are chronic, lifelong conditions that require management rather than a quick cure. [learn more](GST114_U4_T8#GST114_U4_T8_h8)

question: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for anaphylaxis?

options.A: Type III hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: Type I hypersensitivity reaction
options.C: Type II hypersensitivity reaction
options.D: Type IV hypersensitivity reaction

explanation: Anaphylaxis is an immediate Type I IgE-mediated reaction involving mast cells and basophils. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h1)

question: What happens when mast cells degranulate during an allergic reaction?

options.A: Inflammatory mediators are released into tissues
options.B: Antibodies stop the immune system response
options.C: Red blood cells multiply rapidly in vessels
options.D: Platelets clot to close open blood vessels

explanation: Degranulation releases stored chemicals like histamine, which causes sudden widespread blood vessel widening and swelling. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h1)

question: Which group of medications is a common cause of severe anaphylaxis?

options.A: Inhaled corticosteroids
options.B: Fat-soluble vitamins
options.C: Beta-lactam antibiotics
options.D: Oral hypoglycemics

explanation: Antibiotics such as penicillin are well-known triggers for severe allergic drug reactions. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h2)

question: Why do insect stings often cause quick, body-wide reactions in sensitive people?

options.A: Sting sites always develop severe local bacterial infections
options.B: Insect toxins permanently destroy bone marrow cells
options.C: Venom enters the bloodstream directly and spreads
options.D: Venom triggers an immediate drop in body temperature

explanation: When venom is injected directly into tissues or vessels, allergens quickly reach mast cells throughout the body. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h2)

question: Which skin change is most typical of an acute allergic reaction?

options.A: Dry and scaly patches
options.B: Jaundiced skin tone
options.C: Cyanotic nail beds
options.D: Urticaria and flushing

explanation: Hives and skin flushing happen because histamine causes blood vessels to widen and leak fluid into the skin layers. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h3)

question: A patient having an allergic reaction develops wheezing and throat tightness. What causes this?

options.A: Alveolar collapse from fluid overload
options.B: Pleural effusion pressing on lungs
options.C: Pulmonary embolism blocking arteries
options.D: Bronchospasm and laryngeal edema

explanation: Immune chemicals make airway muscles tighten and mucosal tissues swell, which blocks normal breathing. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary assessment framework to use first for a patient in acute anaphylaxis?

options.A: Neurological Glasgow scale
options.B: Sample history and vitals
options.C: Airway, Breathing, Circulation
options.D: Head to toe physical exam

explanation: The ABC approach helps nurses quickly spot and manage life-threatening breathing and circulation problems. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h4)

question: A patient develops noisy breathing and low blood pressure shortly after receiving medication. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Offer the patient a glass of cold oral water
options.B: Leave the bedside to find the attending physician
options.C: Call for emergency assistance and prepare epinephrine
options.D: Document the exact vital signs in the patient chart

explanation: Noisy breathing and low blood pressure point to a life-threatening emergency that needs immediate help and fast medication. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h4)

question: What is the main medication used to treat acute anaphylaxis?

options.A: Salbutamol
options.B: Hydrocortisone
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Diphenhydramine

explanation: Epinephrine works quickly to reverse airway tightening and low blood pressure. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h5)

question: Why is epinephrine injected into the thigh muscle rather than the arm?

options.A: Subcutaneous tissue in the arm delays drug breakdown entirely
options.B: Absorption is faster and more reliable from the vastus lateralis
options.C: Thigh injections cause significantly less local pain for adults
options.D: The deltoid muscle contains too many nerves and blood vessels

explanation: The large thigh muscle has a rich blood supply, which helps the medication enter the bloodstream quickly. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h5)

question: What is a biphasic anaphylactic reaction?

options.A: An allergic response caused by two different drugs at once
options.B: A return of symptoms without re-exposure to the trigger
options.C: A mild skin reaction that turns into a fever days later
options.D: An infection developing after a severe insect sting site

explanation: A biphasic reaction happens when allergic symptoms return hours after the first episode seemed to completely clear up. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h6)

question: How can a nurse tell the difference between a simple fainting spell and anaphylaxis?

options.A: Vasovagal attacks cause severe swelling of the upper airway
options.B: Vasovagal episodes usually feature bradycardia instead of tachycardia
options.C: Vasovagal reactions respond rapidly to intramuscular epinephrine
options.D: Vasovagal syncope always includes widespread itchy hives

explanation: Fainting or vasovagal episodes usually slow the heart rate down, whereas anaphylaxis typically speeds the heart up while dropping blood pressure. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h6)

question: What device should patients with a history of severe allergies carry at all times?

options.A: A digital pulse oximeter
options.B: A metered-dose inhaler
options.C: An epinephrine autoinjector
options.D: A portable blood glucose meter

explanation: Carrying an epinephrine autoinjector allows quick self-treatment if the person accidentally touches or eats their allergen. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h7)

question: Why is it important for someone prone to severe allergies to wear a medical alert bracelet?

options.A: It automatically releases emergency medication when skin temperature rises
options.B: It alerts local food vendors to keep ingredients completely allergen-free
options.C: It prevents the immune system from producing high levels of IgE
options.D: It provides immediate health details if the patient becomes unresponsive

explanation: Medical alert tags give healthcare workers vital allergy information fast if the patient is unable to speak. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of collecting microbiological specimens in clinical practice?

options.A: To identify disease-causing pathogens and guide treatment
options.B: To check for nutritional deficiencies in the patient
options.C: To monitor the daily progression of white blood cells
options.D: To measure the electrolyte balance in body fluids

explanation: Isolating the specific microorganism responsible for an infection allows clinicians to prescribe targeted antimicrobial therapy rather than relying on broad-spectrum drugs. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h1)

question: A poorly collected clinical sample most directly leads to which laboratory outcome?

options.A: Misleading results due to contaminating flora
options.B: An automatic increase in patient white blood cells
options.C: Rapid sterilization of the collected specimen vial
options.D: Immediate destruction of the testing equipment

explanation: Inappropriate collection methods often pick up normal skin bacteria or environmental germs, confusing the lab and resulting in false positives. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h1)

question: When should a nurse perform hand hygiene during the specimen collection process?

options.A: Only if visible blood is present on the nurse's hands
options.B: Before and after patient contact and glove removal
options.C: Only after the laboratory request form is completed
options.D: Before opening the transport medium and at no other time

explanation: Hand hygiene interrupts the transmission of microorganisms and protects both the healthcare worker and the patient. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h2)

question: Universal precautions require treating which category of patient fluids as infectious?

options.A: All biological fluids from every patient
options.B: Body fluids visible contaminated with fresh blood
options.C: Only specimens collected from immune-compromised patients
options.D: Only fluids obtained from confirmed isolation wards

explanation: Universal precautions assume every patient is potentially infectious, regardless of their known diagnosis or infection status. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h2)

question: Why are wooden shaft swabs with cotton tips generally avoided for bacterial cultures?

options.A: They are too flexible to reach deep infected wounds safely
options.B: They automatically sterilize the sample before it reaches the lab
options.C: They contain fatty acids that can inhibit bacterial growth
options.D: They dissolve instantly when exposed to liquid transport media

explanation: Natural cotton fibers and wooden sticks harbor substances toxic to sensitive organisms, leading to false-negative culture results. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h3)

question: What is the primary function of a transport medium like Amies or Stuart gel?

options.A: To keep organisms alive without allowing rapid overgrowth
options.B: To stain the bacteria immediately upon contact in the vial
options.C: To actively kill all normal skin flora present in the sample
options.D: To liquefy thick pus or sputum for easier microscopic reading

explanation: Transport media preserve the viability of fastidious pathogens during transit without letting opportunistic bacteria multiply out of proportion. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h3)

question: Where should a urine sample for culture be collected from an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: The designated needleless sampling port on the tubing
options.B: The bottom drain spout of the plastic collection bag
options.C: Directly from the inner lining of the sterile drainage bag
options.D: By disconnecting the catheter from the drainage tubing

explanation: Urine sitting in the collection bag breeds bacteria over time, so samples must come fresh from the tubing port using aseptic technique. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h4)

question: A patient needs a blood culture drawn to investigate recurring fever spikes. What action reduces skin contaminant risks?

options.A: Wiping the venipuncture site briskly with dry sterile gauze
options.B: Drawing blood immediately after applying alcohol without waiting
options.C: Using a larger gauge needle to flush away surface bacteria
options.D: Allowing the skin antiseptic to dry completely before puncture

explanation: Antiseptics require contact and drying time to kill microorganisms on the skin; puncturing wet skin pushes viable bacteria into the bloodstream sample. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h4)

question: When is the best time of day for a patient to produce a sputum sample for culture?

options.A: Early in the morning before eating or drinking
options.B: Any time of day as long as oral hygiene is skipped
options.C: Late at night right before going to sleep
options.D: Immediately after a heavy midday meal and drink

explanation: Secretions pool overnight in the respiratory tract, making early morning specimens the most concentrated and representative of infection. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h5)

question: Why must a nurse clean a wound with sterile saline before taking a swab for culture?

options.A: To remove surface contaminants and dead skin exudate
options.B: To numb the wound bed and reduce patient pain levels
options.C: To stimulate rapid bleeding that cleans the deep layers
options.D: To chemically sterilize the underlying infected tissue

explanation: Surface pus contains environmental debris and colonizing bacteria that do not represent the actual pathogen causing the deep tissue infection. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h5)

question: At what point during the collection process should the specimen container be labeled?

options.A: After returning from the laboratory drop-off counter
options.B: At the bedside immediately after collection in front of the patient
options.C: Whenever convenient at the end of the work shift
options.D: At the nurses' station before entering the patient room

explanation: Labeling containers away from the bedside or before collection drastically increases the risk of mixing up samples between different patients. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h6)

question: Why is recording current antibiotic therapy on the laboratory request form important?

options.A: It proves to the pharmacy department that drugs were given
options.B: It guides the lab on specialized testing methods required
options.C: It automatically stops the lab from growing normal flora
options.D: It calculates the exact dosage adjustment needed for the patient

explanation: Knowing what drugs are in the patient's system helps microbiologists interpret growth inhibition and select appropriate sensitivity panels. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h6)

question: What is the recommended maximum time window for transporting most bacteriological specimens to the lab?

options.A: Within twenty-four hours of collection
options.B: Within two hours of collection
options.C: Within forty-eight hours of collection
options.D: Exactly one week from collection

explanation: Prompt delivery prevents bacterial overgrowth or pathogen death, ensuring the laboratory culture accurately reflects the patient's infection status. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h7)

question: Which type of microbiological specimen must NOT be placed in a refrigerator during transport delays?

options.A: Blood culture bottles
options.B: Swabs in transport gel
options.C: Sputum collection pots
options.D: Urine specimen cups

explanation: Refrigeration inhibits the growth of certain fastidious bacteria inside blood culture media; these bottles should remain at room temperature. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h7)

question: What immediate action must a nurse take with a used venipuncture needle after blood culture collection?

options.A: Place it on the bedside tray until the procedure is fully finished
options.B: Recap the needle carefully using a two-handed technique
options.C: Break the needle off the syringe barrel before disposal
options.D: Dispose of it directly into a rigid puncture-proof sharps container

explanation: Immediate disposal into a designated sharps container prevents accidental needle-stick injuries to healthcare workers and patients. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h8)

question: How does a contaminated specimen negatively impact patient care?

options.A: It causes the hospital laboratory equipment to malfunction
options.B: It shortens the patient's hospital stay by curing infections faster
options.C: It automatically lowers the patient's blood pressure
options.D: It can trigger unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment

explanation: False-positive results from contamination trick clinicians into treating non-existent infections with powerful drugs, driving resistance and side effects. [learn more](GST114_U5_T1#GST114_U5_T1_h8)

question: What is the primary goal of microbial isolation in the laboratory?

options.A: Separating a single microbe from a mixed population
options.B: Destroying all pathogens present on a surface
options.C: Counting the exact total weight of a sample
options.D: Changing the genetic material of bacteria

explanation: Isolation allows technicians to separate individual species from complex mixtures for independent study. [learn more](GST114_U5_T2#GST114_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why are environmental samples usually described as mixed populations?

options.A: They are completely free of any living organisms
options.B: They only contain viruses and fungi
options.C: They consist of thousands of different microbial species
options.D: They always contain only one bacterial strain

explanation: Natural environments harbour diverse communities of bacteria, fungi, and other microbes living side by side. [learn more](GST114_U5_T2#GST114_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which laboratory equipment is standard for achieving complete sterilisation of media?

options.A: Water bath
options.B: Incubator
options.C: Fume cupboard
